Letter from the CEO
Dick Richelle

7 Vopak Annual Report 2025

Letter from the CEO
Dear reader,
2025 was another year of strong momentum at Vopak. Having successfully achieved many 
of our strategic goals in recent years, we built on this foundation to shift gears to the next 
phase of our Improve, Grow, Accelerate strategy. 
Guided by our strategic objectives, we further improved our portfolio’s financial and 
sustainability performance. In addition, we continued to scale our global portfolio through 
targeted investments in gas and industrial terminals as well as energy transition 
infrastructure. The strong momentum in executing our growth strategy reinforces our 
confidence in achieving our long-term ambition of investing EUR 4 billion by 2030. I believe 
our best-in-class platform enables us to keep improving the performance of our portfolio 
while meeting our ambitious growth targets. 
At the same time, we remain vigilant to changes in our operating landscape across our 
global business. These include increased geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty as 
well as slowing momentum in some aspects of the energy transition. In a complex and 
often challenging marketplace, I am proud of our talented Vopak team for maintaining their 
discipline and focus to deliver value to our stakeholders. 
We remain united by a resilient culture built on our three core pillars: Trust, Collaboration, 
and Courage. They provide us with a shared sense of direction as we navigate the 
evolving energy landscape and the challenges and opportunities it presents. 
Improve
Our business is driven by people with the expertise and dedication to responsibly operate 
bulk liquid infrastructure, alongside a passion for supporting our customers every day. 
As ever, the safety of our people and local communities remains our top priority. This is 
reflected in our continued focus on improving our safety performance, which is a 
fundamental part of our 'Improve' strategic pillar. In 2025, we maintained our high 
standards with a low Total Injury Rate of 0.23 (2024: 0.21) and a consistently low Process 
Safety Event Rate of 0.11 (2024: 0.08). While these metrics demonstrate best-in-class 
performance, they fall short of our ultimate safety ambitions. We remain focused on our 
commitment to driving further improvements in our safety performance.
We also took further steps to address our environmental impact: by the end of the year, 
we had reduced our Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 48% compared to 
our 2021 base-year emissions. Our progress keeps us on track to achieve net zero by 
2050, with an intermediate target of reducing our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 30% by 
2030, whilst accommodating future business growth.
Despite our ongoing efforts, we have not yet realized the level of gender representation to 
which we aspire. In 2025, women held 22% of senior management positions. A diverse and 
inclusive workforce is vital to our long-term success, and we remain deeply committed to 
improving the level of representation.
Customer satisfaction with our services further improved. We achieved a Net Promoter 
Score (NPS) of 82, up from 80 the previous year. This increase reflects our customers’ 
continued appreciation for the service we provide.
Our financial performance further improved in 2025. We saw continued strong demand for 
storage infrastructure across our geographies and markets, reflected in a proportional 
occupancy rate of 91%. Proportional EBITDA, adjusted for currency effects and divestment 
impact, grew by 4.3%. These results translated into an earnings per share increase of 
6.9%, to EUR 3.57, excluding exceptional items. Our continued focus on cash generation 
resulted in proportional operating free cash flow per share growth of 6.6% and a 
proportional operating cash return of 15.6%. For every Euro of proportional EBITDA 
generated, we converted approximately 70 cents into proportional operating free cash 
flow - representing a cash conversion rate of 70%. This robust cash flow allowed us to 
maintain a total net debt to EBITDA ratio of 2.45, even as we significantly ramped up our 
growth investments.
Reflecting our financial health, strong cash generation and our commitment to returning 
value to our shareholders, we distributed EUR 185 million in dividends and completed an 
EUR 100 million share buyback program during the year. Furthermore, on the back of the 
strong results this year, we are pleased to propose a dividend of EUR 1.80 per share. 
Going forward, in line with our disciplined capital allocation policy, we are launching a 
EUR 1.7 billion shareholder distribution program through year-end 2030. This includes an 
annual increase of 5% or more of our dividend per share, with semi-annual payments, and 
a share buyback program of up to EUR 500 million.
8 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Introduction

Grow
Throughout the year, we continued to expand our gas and industrial terminal infrastructure. 
We have significantly ramped up our investments, including a record-level of growth capex 
and more than EUR 500 million in newly secured investment commitments. 
These investments are underpinned by long-term customer commitments.
In Western Canada, work continued on the large-scale liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) REEF 
export terminal and we are further optimizing its throughput capacity. Our REEF terminal 
will create vital connections and logistical efficiencies between Canada and the 
Asia-Pacific region. In India, supported by our successful initial public offering, AVTL is 
enabling the transition to lower-carbon fuels like LPG. During the year, AVTL commissioned 
multiple expansions across its Mangalore, Pipavav, and Mumbai terminals and invested in 
further expansions in multiple locations. In the Netherlands, construction of the 4th tank at 
the GATE terminal is progressing well. Once commissioned, this expansion will further 
enhance the terminal’s LNG import capabilities, playing a vital role in strengthening 
Europe’s energy security. Furthermore, we announced multiple expansion projects during 
the year in China, Thailand, and Colombia, increasing capacity and adapting to evolving 
customer demands.
Accelerate
With our unique capabilities to enable a future-focused energy mix, Vopak remains 
committed to seizing the opportunities provided by the energy transition and accelerating 
our contribution as a partner in lower-carbon solutions. 
In 2025, we continued to advance the development of strategically located land at the port 
of Antwerp in Belgium, which provides opportunities to store green methanol and ammonia. 
In addition, Vopak’s Alemoa terminal is expanding at the port of Santos that will serve the 
fast-growing ethanol market in Brazil. An investment decision was also taken at the PT2SB 
Terminal in Malaysia to expand capacity to support the storage of biofuels feedstocks and 
products. 
As our customers pursue the decarbonization of their business activities, we see an 
increased need for CO₂ infrastructure. In the Netherlands, we aim to develop an open- 
access terminal with our partners that can store and handle CO₂ before it is injected into 
depleted gas fields offshore. 
9 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Introduction

We have also made progress in the electricity-storage market. We have acquired 100% of a 
battery development company in Groningen, the Netherlands. This acquisition provides 
Vopak with critical assets – including land, a 300 MW grid connection, and all permits – 
to construct its own utility-scale lithium-ion battery system.
With our capabilities and strong track record, I believe Vopak can drive progress in the 
energy transition by strengthening our existing network, repurposing infrastructure, 
leveraging our strong relationships with partners and customers, and undertaking 
brownfield and greenfield expansions in the area of energy transition.
Through Vopak WeConnect, we support local development initiatives in the communities 
where we operate. In 2025, our teams around the world developed and delivered 25 
WeConnect projects, fostering positive, value-adding relationships with local communities. 
Creating and capturing new opportunities
While we are proud of our achievements over the past year, we remain committed to 
further improvement in the years ahead. In 2026, we will continue to build on our 
world-class network and capabilities to deliver for our customers.
I would like to thank our entire team – as well as our trusted partners around the globe – 
for their invaluable contributions as we work together to help the world flow forward.
Thank you for your contribution, and stay safe.
Dick Richelle
Chairman of the Executive Board and CEO of Royal Vopak

11 Vopak Annual Report 2025

Our purpose
We help the world flow forward
Vopak delivers safe, reliable, and efficient storage of essential products for everyday life. For over four centuries, we have been working closely 
with businesses and communities to improve our services year after year. As the world’s energy needs evolve, our talented people drive 
progress by advancing partnerships that accelerate the development of infrastructure solutions that will support lower-carbon solutions.
We help...
We embrace our role as a critical link in global energy and chemical supply chains, 
delivering on our promise day in, day out, thanks to the enduring strength of our assets. 
Serving more than 1,000 customers, we always search for the optimal infrastructure 
solution to help customers thrive and unlock new opportunities. Through Vopak 
WeConnect, we also support local development initiatives in the communities where we 
operate.
...the world...
With storage infrastructure in 21 countries and evolving partnerships around the world, we 
know how to do business on a global scale and with a future-focused approach. 
We embrace – and are expanding – our role as an initiator and enabler of positive change. 
This means taking responsibility for tackling global challenges such as the energy transition 
and ensuring security of supply across multiple markets and locations.
…flow forward
The liquids and gases we handle and store with care have one thing in common: they are 
ultimately on a journey to play a key role in the global economy, at the right place and at 
the right time. Across generations and cultures, we continue to support the global flow 
between supply and demand, as well as the flow of ideas and innovations that will enable a 
better tomorrow.
12 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our purpose & strategy

Shaping the future
13 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our purpose & strategy

Our strategy
At Vopak, generating growing and predictable cash flows serves as the foundation of our strategy. To achieve this objective, we apply 
disciplined portfolio management, continuously improve the performance of our existing asset base whilst allocating capital toward strategic 
growth opportunities, ensuring we are well-positioned to create enduring value for our stakeholders.
Shifting gears in 2025
Building on the solid foundation established in previous years, we shifted gears in 2025 to 
execute the next phase of our strategic roadmap, which is anchored by three integrated 
pillars: Improve, Grow, and Accelerate. 
Improve
We are committed to improving the financial and sustainability performance of our 
portfolio, as evidenced by our strong execution in recent years. As ever, the safety of our 
people and local communities remains our top priority, representing a critical license to 
operate that underpins every aspect of our strategy and execution. In addition, we are 
committed to improving our environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance by 
reducing emissions, preventing life-changing injuries, and eliminating spills. This foundation 
of responsible execution has enabled us to realize significant financial progress. Driven by 
enhanced cash generation and operational excellence, we have raised our portfolio 
operating cash return target to above 13%. To ensure a resilient financial position, we have 
also established a proportional leverage range of 2.5x to 3.0x.
Grow
Growing our base in gas and industrial terminals is the cornerstone of our long-term growth 
strategy. We have demonstrated strong momentum executing our 'Grow' strategic pillar, 
committing EUR 1.7 billion proportional growth capex since we set the investment ambition 
in 2022. Building on this milestone, we have increased our investment ambition to 
EUR 2.6 billion through 2030. This positions us to pursue further growth in segments that 
offer attractive, long-term contracted returns and aligns directly with the structural trends 
shaping the future of energy and manufacturing markets. 
Accelerate
Despite an increasingly volatile geopolitical and energy landscape, we remain committed to 
investing EUR 1.4 billion by 2030 in infrastructure that supports the energy transition. 
We are investing in new infrastructure solutions while maintaining a selective approach to 
secure a risk-return profile consistent with our core business. Our focus is on key 
infrastructure solutions, including low-carbon fuels and sustainable feedstocks, ammonia 
as a hydrogen carrier, liquid CO₂, and battery energy storage.

Accelerating growth in 
India through a strategic 
partnership and public 
listing
"The successful IPO strengthens AVTL’s position as a market 
leader, empowering independent funding for ambitious growth 
in India’s rapidly expanding energy landscape."
Following a successful IPO, AVTL is positioned for significant expansion. 
Investments are being made in a greenfield terminal in Mumbai and India’s first

Our business
Vopak provides safe and efficient infrastructure solutions and services for bulk liquids and gases through our global network of strategically 
located storage terminals. Our world-class network plays a vital role in balancing the supply and demand of products that are crucial for energy 
and manufacturing markets.
Business model
We own and operate storage terminals that enable customers to safely store their bulk 
liquids, gas, and chemicals products. We provide access to our storage capacity, primarily 
through contracted storage fees, often structured as long-term, ‘take-or-pay’ agreements 
that ensure predictable, steady cash flows. Beyond providing storage capacity, our value 
proposition centers on specialized services—such as blending and heating—essential to 
preserving the integrity and quality of the products we store.
Global network
Our unparalleled global network, consisting of 75 terminals located at 50 ports across 21 
countries, enables us to efficiently meet the growing demand for bulk liquid and gas 
storage infrastructure. We are proud to serve over 1,000 customers globally, providing 
expert storage solutions for more than 250 different products. We believe this 
diversification is key to the stability of our business, limiting volatility by capturing 
opportunities across different market cycles.
17 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Role in the value chain
At its core, our infrastructure addresses a fundamental imbalance in the global energy and 
manufacturing markets: production and consumption rarely align in terms of timing, scale or 
location. Our terminals have a critical role in matching supply with demand, ensuring 
market stability. However, our role in the supply chain extends beyond balancing supply 
and demand. As products move through the supply chain, they must transition between 
different modes of transport—from deep-sea vessels to regional pipelines, railcars, or 
trucks. Our terminals act as the critical interface where these changes in modality occur, 
allowing for the safe and efficient transfer of product. In addition, we provide the critical 
infrastructure and operational capabilities for managing the integrity of volatile and 
hazardous products, ensuring their safe and efficient flow through the supply chain.
Our diversified global infrastructure portfolio is strategically positioned to fulfill distinct 
roles within the energy and manufacturing supply chains. We operate import and export 
terminals as essential gateways for regions with structural supply imbalances, while our 
large-scale Hub terminals at major maritime crossroads facilitate critical transshipment, 
blending, and market optimization. To further support the supply chain, our distribution 
terminals provide localized access to end-markets, while our industrial terminals offer deep 
infrastructure integration into petrochemical clusters of our customers, managing complex 
feedstock and rundown logistics via dedicated pipeline connections.
Our status as an independent provider of storage capacity ensures neutral, reliable access 
for all parties. By utilizing our shared infrastructure, customers benefit from economies of 
scale, spreading the costs of world-class safety, technology, and regulatory compliance 
across a multi-user platform.
Facilitating progress
Our strategic positioning at the heart of global supply chains allows us to facilitate evolving 
market demands. As the global population grows and the standard of living rises, energy 
and manufacturing markets will continue to meet growing demand. We enable this growth 
by providing the essential storage capacity and connectivity that ensure the secure, 
reliable flow of vital products.
Simultaneously, we leverage our existing footprint and technical expertise to facilitate the 
ongoing energy transition. This involves converting our assets to store lower-carbon 
products and biofuels, and working with our joint venture partners, customers, and the 
communities in which we operate to actively shape a sustainable future.

Our terminals
20 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Gas
There is a growing need for lower-carbon energy solutions. Natural 
gas offers affordable energy and security of supply while actively 
supporting the energy transition by replacing more carbon-intensive 
sources such as wood, coal, and oil.
As global production and consumption locations continue to diverge, liquefied natural gas 
(LNG) has become a critical link in the supply chain-essential for maintaining global energy 
security and affordability. The global LNG market is expected to continue growing, driven 
by substantial supply increases, particularly from the United States. Separately, the global 
liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supply will be boosted by rising gas production, notably in 
the United States, Canada, and the Middle East. The bulk of this production will be used as 
feedstock for industry, particularly in China, while growing demand will also come from 
emerging residential markets, especially in India. Expanding our gas storage capacity is a 
key strategic priority that supports growing demand across the power, residential, and 
petrochemical sectors. 
 
21 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Industrial
Refineries and petrochemical processing facilities supply the critical 
energy and chemical products vital to modern society, meeting 
continuously growing demand. 
As the leader in industrial terminals, our infrastructure accommodates growing 
manufacturing demand, driven by a rising global population and an expanding middle 
class. The industrial terminal model involves a single operator serving several customer 
plants, providing integrated storage for feedstocks and run-down products. By optimizing 
infrastructure and logistics within these complexes, we ensure seamless flow between 
various plants. Our industrial terminals support manufacturing markets in key regions, 
including the United States, Asia, and the Middle East, and their continued growth remains 
a central strategic priority for our company.
22 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Chemicals
Chemicals play a critical role in countless industries and supply 
chains, with growing global demand for chemical products closely 
linked to increasing economic activity, and particularly growing GDP 
per capita in emerging markets.
We facilitate the global flow of chemicals, ensuring products move efficiently from 
production centers to end-markets. Our chemical terminal network supports petrochemical 
producers and traders by enabling the export, import, make-bulk, and break-bulk of 
various bulk and specialty chemicals. Despite ongoing weakness in chemical markets, 
primarily driven by a mixture of overcapacity, compressed margins and lower demand, 
long-term demand for petrochemicals is projected to grow.
23 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Oil
Continuous growth in global energy demand, driven by economic and 
demographic factors, creates a persistent and fundamental need for 
stable and reliable energy sources. 
Global oil demand is undergoing a geographical and structural transformation. 
Consumption continues to rise across fast-growing regions such as South-East Asia, the 
Middle East, and Africa. By contrast, demand is stabilizing or exhibiting a moderate decline 
in OECD countries, particularly in Europe, driven by the cumulative impact of energy 
transition policies, efficiency gains, and slower demographic growth. Despite the ongoing 
energy transition, oil remains a critically important component of the global energy mix, 
particularly for transportation and the production of petrochemical feedstocks, 
underscoring the continued need for its secure supply. Our global infrastructure is 
therefore strategically vital to support diverse global demand for storage infrastructure and 
logistics solutions.
24 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Investing in LPG 
infrastructure in western 
Canada
"This landmark investment supports our Grow strategic pillar, 
utilizing a highly strategic location to connect Canadian energy 
exports to growing demand in Asia."
As Vopak’s largest single investment, REEF exemplifies our ambition to grow in gas 
terminals. Developed with AltaGas, this large-scale LPG export facility in Prince 
Rupert offers the shortest route to Asia. Construction is progressing on schedule for 
2026 commissioning, with additional throughput capacity already approved for 2027. 
The development of this essential infrastructure aims to create long-term value and 
ensure security of supply – a key example of strategic growth in gas infrastructure 
connecting global markets.
25 Vopak Annual Report 2025

Our value creation
At Vopak, we aim to create long-term value for all of our stakeholders – from our 
customers and business partners to our shareholders, employees, and local communities.
Customers
In 2025, Vopak continued to provide infrastructure solutions, whilst working with 
customers to drive progress in the energy transition. Across industries and geographies, 
we provided safe, reliable, and efficient storage solutions for essential products, and 
handled products safely and efficiently. As measured by our Net Promoter Score (NPS) 
survey, our customer loyalty improved in 2025, reaching 82 (2024: 80). This increase 
reflects our customers’ continued appreciation for the service we provide.
Employees and contractors
As a leading global employer, we are committed to providing attractive, fairly paid work 
opportunities for employees and contractors in the regions where we operate 
worldwide. In 2025, we continued to adhere to the living wage principle across all 
locations. In line with our growing focus on safety and sustainability, we also took further 
steps to ensure a healthy, safe, and inclusive working environment at all our terminals and 
sites. These efforts are reflected in our process safety event rate of 0.11, and Total Injury 
Rate (3 year rolling average) of 0.20, per 200,000 hours worked.
Shareholders
In 2025, we demonstrated our long-term commitment to create and distribute value for our 
shareholders by paying healthy dividends totaling EUR 185 million and by executing a 
EUR 100 million share buyback program. We also continued to engage closely with our 
shareholder community, including at our 2025 Capital Markets Day and various roadshows 
and meetings organized throughout the year, with a focus on Europe and North America.
Government and authorities
As a multinational company that plays a key role in global supply chains, it is fundamental 
to our license to operate that we maintain positive relationships with local governments 
and authorities. In 2025, we continued to pay fair taxes in the jurisdictions where we 
operate. Meanwhile, we continued to comply with local safety, health, and environmental 
laws, while supporting energy security and driving the energy transition in these regions.
26 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

Local communities
Vopak seeks to foster positive, value-adding relationships with the local communities in 
which we operate. Our value creation includes hiring and training local people, stimulating 
economic growth through investment, and supporting local communities. In 2025, our 
teams around the world developed and delivered 25 WeConnect projects. The core 
mission of Vopak WeConnect is to encourage and support our company and our joint 
venture employees in setting up volunteering projects near Vopak locations, with a focus 
on helping youngsters and contributing to more sustainable communities.
Business partners and suppliers
We collaborate with suppliers and partners at different points in our value chains. 
In particular, we prioritize partnerships that can accelerate the development of new energy 
infrastructure solutions. In 2025, we continued to form new value-adding joint ventures, 
including with OQ in Oman. We also created new opportunities for business partners by 
expanding capacity and switching to more sustainable feedstocks at our terminals. 
Throughout the year, we continued to ensure the fair and responsible treatment of all our 
suppliers, who range from global IT providers to local service and construction companies.
Value creation model
Our value creation model, which is presented on the next page, describes both the 
resources we consume (inputs) and the value we create or deplete during the course of 
our business (outputs). Importantly, this model considers key socioeconomic issues, 
allowing us to identify instances in which a particular strategy or investment may create 
value for one stakeholder group but reduce it for another. The table below shows the

Our responsible business conduct
Vopak fosters a culture rooted in trust, collaboration, and courage. We seek to create a responsible, inclusive environment where employees, 
contractors, and suppliers feel valued and empowered. This commitment extends to the communities where we operate and reflects our 
dedication to ethical, sustainable practices.
Our culture serves as a blueprint for our actions. It encourages open communication, 
thoughtful analysis, and the conviction to navigate challenges with integrity. 
This foundation allows us to adapt to a changing world while upholding high standards.
Central to this approach is our Code of Conduct, which sets clear expectations for ethical 
behavior, covering areas such as anti-corruption, human rights, and health and safety. 
This code applies globally to all employees, contractors, suppliers, and partners. 
We reinforce these standards through mandatory training and regular reporting to ensure 
accountability and transparency.
Sustainability at Vopak
To deliver on our purpose – We help the world flow forward – we serve the needs of the 
present while safeguarding the ability of future generations to thrive. We develop 
infrastructure that supports essential products for today and the future. In doing so, we 
prioritize the safety, health, and well-being of people and the environment.
We aim to create value for all stakeholders, including customers, shareholders, employees, 
and local communities. Our decisions balance current interests with 
long-term sustainability. The decisions we make today should therefore serve the current 
and long-term interests of society, as well as the sustainability and development of current 
and future generations. We outline our progress in the Sustainability section of this annual 
report.
For details on how our management oversees environmental, social, and governance (ESG) 
topics – including risk management and incentive schemes – please refer to the General 
disclosures in the Sustainability Statement in this report for more details.
Vopak’s double materiality assessment
Vopak prioritizes transparency and sustainability. In line with the Corporate Sustainability 
Reporting Directive (CSRD), we conducted a double materiality assessment (DMA) to 
identify material ESG topics. We analyzed how these issues affect our business (financial 
materiality) and how our operations impact the world around us (impact materiality).
We engaged internal and external stakeholders to review relevant impacts, risks, and 
opportunities. This process identified six material topics that are central to our business 
strategy and our purpose. For more details on our DMA, please refer to the General 
disclosures and materiality of sustainability statement.
We mapped these material topics to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards 
(ESRS). The primary standards identified were E1, E2, S1, S2, and G1. We present the notes 
for these topics as our ‘Sustainability Statement’, prepared in accordance with CSRD 
requirements. Where data points related to material topics appear elsewhere in this report, 
we incorporated them by reference.
Operational safety and health
Vopak prioritizes the safe handling of all products within our global terminal network. 
We maintain high safety standards, promote a culture of safety awareness and 
responsibility among our workforce, and actively mitigate workplace risks to protect our 
employees, contractors, and neighboring communities. Our commitment to safety is 
embedded in our global standards, including our Fundamentals on Safety, and applies to 
all employees and contractors. 
29 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our business & value creation

In the daily operation and maintenance of our terminals, we conduct routine and 
non-routine activities that are managed through our control of work standards and 
procedures. Each of our employees, contractors (general or specific contingent workers), 
and service providers must adhere to our safety, health, and environment (SHE) policies 
and standards. These requirements are formalized through employment and service 
contracts and supported by training at all locations. 
All incidents – no matter how minor – are reported, as are all near misses. Reports are 
entered directly into our incident reporting system, Enablon. We systematically report and 
investigate any high-potential near misses, work-related injuries, fatalities, and 
occupational illnesses, as well as process safety incidents such as spills, contaminations, 
and fires. This helps us to further improve our SHE performance. We prioritize learning from 
incidents by sharing incident learnings and encouraging their implementation across all 
sites where applicable. 
Through our ongoing development of the Vopak Trust & Verify program, we proactively 
align our fieldwork with our procedures and encourage a culture of personal accountability 
for safety at all levels of the company. 
We prioritize process safety through rigorous audits, a comprehensive maintenance 
program, and systematic risk assessments. We foster a safety-first culture, conduct annual 
emergency response tests, and collaborate with local authorities to ensure preparedness 
for any incident.
In addition to our own staff, we employ thousands of contractors across our locations. 
The contractors outnumber our Vopak employees. Contractors often work on construction 
sites or maintenance projects, and we work directly with them on health & safety standards 
and training, human rights, ethics, and integrity. These expectations are outlined in our 
Code of Conduct and Supplier Code. Contractors and suppliers must also adhere to our 
SHE and Sustainability Policies, as well as our living wage approach. They must also adhere 
to international human and labor rights standards as set out by the International Labour 
Organization (ILO).
Please refer to Note 4. Process safety and prevention of spills, and Note 5. Occupational 
health and safety, in the Sustainability Statement for more details.
Environment management
We aim to reduce our environmental impact to drive progress and shape a sustainable 
future. We view this as a vital responsibility to the communities in which we operate. 
Our robust environmental management process aligns with internal standards, including 
our Environmental Impact Assessment and Soil and Groundwater Management 
frameworks. We aim to reduce our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 30% by 2030, 
compared to 2021 base-year emissions, whilst accommodating future business growth.  
To mitigate our VOC emissions, we have implemented improvement programs at our 
terminals to further reduce emissions of volatile organic compounds and substances of 
very high concern (SVHCs). Beyond compliance, we assess these emissions to understand 
and mitigate their broader impact on society and public health.

Governance and risk management
Vopak is committed to conducting business with integrity and in compliance with laws and 
regulations. The company has a comprehensive Code of Conduct that covers all relevant 
topics.  
We have implemented a third-party speak-up software system that allows employees, 
contractors, value chain workers, and other stakeholders to report ethical concerns or 
dilemmas. Our rules and procedures related to anti-corruption or anti-bribery are set out 
in our Anti-Bribery and Corruption (ABC) Policy, which is accessible to all employees. 
We actively engage with stakeholders at local, national, and European levels to support the 
development of essential energy infrastructure, particularly for new energy sources and 
sustainable feedstocks. 
Doing business involves taking risks. We strive to be a successful and respected company 
and seek to take a balanced approach to risk. Risk management is an essential element of 
our corporate governance and strategy development. Our risk management framework is in 
line with the Enterprise Risk Management – Integrated Framework of COSO.
Overall, the risk profile of the company has not materially changed compared to 2024. 
The execution of the growth strategy is deemed neutral from a risk perspective, with 
promising prospects for profitable projects in the 'Grow' pillar. The 'Accelerate' part of the 
strategy holds good potential for converting storage capacity to low-carbon products, 
while there are also opportunities in, amongst others, battery energy storage solutions 
(BESS) and biofuels.
Geopolitical risks have increased again. The year 2025 was defined by a significant shift 
in the United States' foreign policy. Following the inauguration of a new administration, 
Washington implemented broad tariffs on imports, triggering friction with global trading 
partners and shifts in trade flows. Consequently, the geopolitical environment has become 
more turbulent, with economic uncertainty and geopolitical volatility converging. This  
uncertainty is reducing companies' ability to plan and invest for the long-term, which is also 
evident in Vopak’s larger business environment. 
Market risk remains an inherent aspect of Vopak's business model. While the risks related 
to the physical effects of climate change have not changed, they continue to pose 
potential risks to a number of terminals. Trends related to safety, health, environment, laws 
and regulations, people, and cybersecurity are evaluated as neutral, and measures are in 
place to mitigate risks. Supported by a strong consolidated balance sheet, Vopak’s access 
to capital is safeguarded, but the longer-term risks remain.

Financial performance
IFRS Measures -including exceptional items-
Revenues
During 2025, Vopak generated revenues of EUR 1,298.9 million, compared to EUR 1,315.6 
million in 2024. Excluding negative currency translation effects of EUR 32.5 million and 
divestment impacts of EUR 4.8 million, the increase was EUR 20.6 million (1.6%), driven by 
growth projects contribution and existing business growth.
The average occupancy rate for Vopak’s subsidiaries (i.e. excluding joint ventures and 
associates) in 2025 was 91%, a 1% decrease compared to a 92% average occupancy rate 
in 2024.
Expenses
In 2025, personnel expenses were EUR 342.4 million, an increase of EUR 1.5 million (0.4%) 
compared to EUR 340.9 million in 2024. Excluding positive currency translation effects of 
EUR 6.5 million and divestment impacts of EUR 1.0 million, the increase of EUR 9.0 million 
was mainly driven by the higher remuneration in accordance with the Collective Labor 
Agreement (CLA) and higher cost for short- and long-term incentive plans plus 
organizational integration and restructuring charges. During 2025, Vopak employed, in 
FTEs, an average of 3,433 employees (2024: 3,512), excluding joint ventures and 
associates.
Other operating expenses increased by EUR 9.1 million (2.9%) to EUR 330.4 million 
(2024: EUR 321.2 million). Excluding positive currency translation effects of EUR 8.3 million 
and divestment impacts of EUR 1.2 million, the increase was EUR 18.7 million.
Result joint ventures and associates
In 2025, the result of joint ventures and associates was EUR 226.3 million, a decrease of 
EUR 27.6 million (10.8%) compared to EUR 253.9 million in 2024. Currency translation had 
a negative effect of EUR 8.2 million. The decrease was mainly driven by an exceptional 
gain of EUR 29.7 million recorded in 2024 related to the reversal of the impairment in SPEC 
cash-generating unit, partly offset by improved performance of joint ventures and 
associates. This includes a gain of EUR 22 million related to a commercial resolution in 
PT2SB reported in the Asia & Middle East Business Unit. 
Depreciation and amortization
Depreciation and amortization charges were EUR 315.2 million, which is EUR 7.8 million 
(2.5%) higher than the prior year (2024: EUR 307.4 million). Adjusted for positive currency 
translation effects of EUR 6.4 million, depreciation and amortization charges increased by 
EUR 14.2 million largely driven by commissioning of projects in the Netherlands and USA & 
Canada Business Units.
Impairments
In 2025, net impairment reversals of EUR 146.9 million were recognized, including a 
EUR 180.7 million reversal of an impairment reported in the Business Unit Netherlands and 
allocated to property, plant and equipment of the Europoort cash-generating unit. An 
impairment charge of EUR 31.9 million was recognized for the Vopak Gas Terminal (VGT) 
cash-generating unit related to challenging market conditions impacting our customers' 
petrochemical refinery activities in the region. An impairment of EUR 1.9 million relates to 
idled leased HQ building assets where the carrying amount is no longer supported by the 
expected sublease income.
In 2024, an impairment charge of EUR 10.1 million was recognized for the Ningbo 
cash-generating unit, following plans to remove terminal capacity to position for future 
developments in the infrastructure landscape of the port. Further, impairment charges of 
EUR 64.9 million were recognized, consisting of the write down of business development 
costs of EUR 6.7 million reported in Business Unit Netherlands and an impairment charge 
of EUR 58.2 million for the Veracruz cash-generating unit.
Cash flows from operating activities and working capital
Cash flows from operating activities (gross) were EUR 967.4 million in 2025 
(2024: EUR 947.5 million). The increase of EUR 19.9 million was mainly the result of the 
realized value adjustments of derivative financial instruments of EUR 46.5 million, partially 
offset by movements in working capital.

Sustainability performance
Vopak drives sustainability through an ambitious, performance-led roadmap focused on environment, society, and governance. Safety remains 
our priority. We actively contribute to the energy transition by investing in infrastructure that stores and handles lower-carbon products while 
reducing our environmental and carbon footprints.
Our Sustainability Roadmap
We continue to execute our Sustainability Roadmap and reinforce our commitment to 
long-term value creation. This recently revised roadmap builds on previous progress while 
integrating the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and insights from our Double 
Materiality Assessment. These updates ensure our efforts remain aligned with evolving 
best practices.
Our Sustainability Roadmap defines specific environmental, social, and governance (ESG) 
actions for the topics that matter most to our stakeholders and our business. It outlines 
how we are shifting gears to transform our portfolio toward lower-carbon conventional 
products as well as zero- and low-carbon energies. We incorporate these priorities into our 
investment decisions, business agendas, and performance goals. Translating key 
sustainability priorities into actionable steps aligns them with our annual budget cycles, 
work programs, and key performance indicators, thereby fostering long-term value creation 
and accountability.
Caring about our impact on society
Safety is the highest priority at Vopak. Our care extends from our colleagues to the 
communities where we operate. We believe that all safety incidents are preventable and 
strive for zero injuries. Our Total Injury Rate (TIR) was 0.23 (2024: 0.21). This outcome falls 
short of our safety ambitions. We remain steadfast in our commitment to our goal of zero 
fatalities, life-changing injuries, and occupational illnesses. We investigate all incidents and 
implement lessons learned across our network to prevent recurrence.
We maintained a strong track record in process safety, achieving a Process Safety Event 
Rate of 0.11 (2024: 0.08). For details, please refer to Note 5. Occupational health and 
safety in the Sustainability Statement for more details.

Operating performance
At Vopak, we aspire to be our customers’ partner of choice and serve them in a way that sets them up for success in their business. Maintaining 
a strong operating performance supports this ambition by creating a solid foundation on which to grow our customer base, specifically as we 
expand our base in gas and industrial terminals and accelerate towards energy transition infrastructure. 
Global standards
Our global operations are based on detailed, blueprinted processes that are continuously 
improved through an integrated set of KPIs. We rely on over 80 Vopak global standards 
that are developed and applicable to all terminals. We also maintain communities of 
subject matter experts across our terminal network, ensuring unrivaled access to 
knowledge and experience.
Quality of service
Delivering the highest service quality and improving the performance of our terminal 
network are essential. We carefully monitor customer and third-party reception of our 
services through consistent daily interactions, structured periodic operational review 
meetings, and customer satisfaction measurements such as the NPS score. We have a 
proven track record in storing products essential to the energy transition, including 
ammonia, methanol, and biodiesel. This record establishes our credible capacity to provide 
the necessary infrastructure for these and similar new products destined for use in energy 
and manufacturing markets.
In 2025, we continued to invest across our network to ensure high service levels. 
We enhanced and deployed our suite of digital solutions to operate our terminals, resulting 
in our purpose-built, self-developed terminal management system being used at 32 Vopak 
and joint venture terminals at the end of the year. Following this year’s successful 
implementations, we have decommissioned the legacy system. We connected with our 
customers via system-to-system interfaces, reducing human error, increasing accessibility, 
and ensuring first-time-right delivery. Furthermore, we continued to invest in enhancing 
the cyber resilience of our IT and operational technology environments.

Accelerating towards energy transition 
infrastructure
Investing in energy transition infrastructure is a strategic priority at Vopak. We remain dedicated to building the pathways that drive global 
progress. As we develop our global portfolio, we are focused on several key areas including low-carbon fuels and sustainable feedstocks, 
ammonia as a hydrogen carrier, CO₂ infrastructure, and battery energy storage.
Low-carbon fuels and feedstocks
Demand for lower-carbon fuels continues to grow, supported by government 
decarbonization policies around the world. Biofuel production is shifting toward advanced 
feedstocks, and demand is expanding beyond the traditional road segment into the 
aviation and marine segments. Vopak contributes to the supply chain by storing feedstock, 
storing the final products, and providing storage before distribution to the end market.
We continue to expand our presence in the biofuel market, supporting projects across the 
supply chain with terminal connections in strategic locations. These include the Pengerang 
Terminal (Two) Sdn. Bhd. ('PT2SB') terminal in Malaysia, where a final investment decision 
(FID) was made to expand capacity by 272k cbm to store biofuels feedstocks and finished 
products. This new capacity will be industrially linked to a biorefinery operated by an 
existing customer and is backed by a long-term take-or-pay agreement.
55 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Our performance

In Alemoa, Brazil, an FID was taken to develop 66k cbm of capacity for low-carbon fuels 
and feedstocks to support the local ethanol market. In the Netherlands, the Vlaardingen 
terminal saw the commissioning of repurposed capacity for feedstocks as part of our 
ongoing strategy to repurpose existing capacity for low-carbon fuels and feedstocks.
Ammonia and hydrogen
Vopak is developing infrastructure solutions to enable the export, transport, import, and 
storage of zero- and low-carbon hydrogen and ammonia. Vopak's role involves storing the 
ammonia carrier after hydrogen production and storing the carrier for the subsequent 
release of hydrogen before distribution to the end market. We are exploring multiple 
alternatives for the transportation and storage of hydrogen, recognizing that ammonia will 
likely be the primary hydrogen carrier in the years to come. We currently store and handle 
ammonia at six terminals around the world, and a seventh independent terminal of AVTL is 
under construction in India. We are uniquely positioned to develop terminals on both sides 
of new energy supply chains through open-access infrastructure. We are developing 
projects to export ammonia from production sites on the US Gulf Coast and in the Middle 
East. In terms of imports, we are well-positioned in key demand regions such as Asia and 
Northwest Europe.
Carbon capture, utilization, and storage
Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) is an important instrument with the 
potential to abate large quantities of CO₂ emissions in the future. CCUS involves capturing 
CO₂ from point-source emitters and transporting it to permanent storage facilities, either 
onshore or offshore. Alternatively, captured CO₂ can be used as a circular feedstock for 
the production of e-fuels and other products.
We are pursuing open-access terminal infrastructure for the temporary storage and 
handling of liquefied CO₂. Transporting liquefied CO₂ by ship will enable customers to 
connect to permanent storage or utilization facilities. In the Netherlands, the CO₂next 
project in Rotterdam, a consortium led by Vopak, is an example of our efforts in this area. 
We are also pursuing the development of CO₂ import and export terminals, preferably in 
the vicinity of existing terminals in the portfolio.
Battery energy storage
Electrons play  an increasingly important role in the global energy mix. This trend is largely 
driven by the ongoing electrification of key areas such as (industrial) heating and 
transportation. In addition, both the rapid development and adoption of artificial 
intelligence solutions and the continuing shift toward digital infrastructure are contributing 
significantly to global electricity demand. Vopak is involved in battery energy storage by 
linking intermittent renewable power production to the high-voltage grid.
Electricity is increasingly being generated by renewable energy sources. 
These energy sources create daily and multi-day fluctuations in energy supply due to 
weather-dependent intermittency. As a result, battery energy storage is required to 
integrate renewables more effectively into the system. Batteries allow for time-shifting 
surplus generation, balancing prediction errors, and mitigating power system failures. 
For Vopak, independent utility-scale storage projects offer an opportunity to diversify and 
add value to the world’s energy markets and the energy transition, supported by our 
financial strength, global presence, project development methodology, and reputation.
We are already pursuing opportunities to provide independent utility-scale electricity 
storage. We operate 15 MW/30 MWh lithium-ion battery storage in the Texas market in the 
United States. We see opportunities for additional battery projects in our portfolio in 2026, 
including both stand-alone projects and projects at our existing terminals. In addition, we 
are continuously exploring acquisition opportunities for projects or assets that offer a clear, 
long-term path to value creation.

Value chain, our core role versus our limits
We believe sustainability requires managing our influence across the entire value chain. 
Through our DMA, we systematically evaluate IROs within both our upstream supply chain 
and downstream customer and consumer base. 
This commitment is codified in policies and targets that address our broader environmental 
and social footprint beyond our direct operations. For instance:
Our customers are producers, manufacturers, distributors, governments, and traders. 
They include leading international, regional, and national chemical and energy companies. 
Our terminals directly connect with national grids and distribution networks to ensure 
timely dispatch. We are responsible for the physical integrity, safety, and regulatory 
compliance of the products while they are in our terminals.
We have a well-established client screening process and checks, conducted when a 
product enters storage and when it is released. However, our effective influence largely 
ends when the product leaves our terminal. The subsequent complex market – where the 
product is traded, blended, and redistributed – means Vopak has no direct control over the 
ultimate use or final end-destination. Full downstream traceability becomes impossible for 
us as an infrastructure provider. Similarly, we cannot determine or influence the 
environmental footprint of the use phase emissions of the products we store and handle.
We also rely on diverse suppliers, from global qualified vendors to local service and 
construction contractors, prioritizing long-term partnerships built on quality and safety. 
We recognize the actual and perceived societal and human rights risks in our value chain 
(e.g., decent work, labor rights, occupational safety). We are actively working to screen 
existing and prospective suppliers and contractors against these standards. For details,

Financial materiality (outside-in): This dimension assesses how sustainability issues

countries in which we operate and inform our due diligence procedures.
For the financial materiality assessment, internal stakeholders were instrumental in 
identifying and scoring risks and opportunities. This collaborative effort included the 
Internal Audit team focusing on risks, and contributors from business development, 
financial analysis, global operations and customer care, and the Strategic Committee 
focusing on opportunities.
Analysis and results
The topics were plotted on the materiality matrix (ESRS 2, DR IRO-1). Our scoring 
methodology, similar to a traditional risk management approach, is based on the likelihood 
of occurrence and the magnitude of potential financial effects. To avoid underestimating a 
topic's importance, we plotted the highest score for either risk or opportunity, rather than 
an average.
The results were presented to the EB and various Executive Vice Presidents for insight and 
validation of the scores and underlying rationale. These discussions helped define the 
thresholds for the final matrix categorization:

A threshold of 3 (on a scale of 0-5) was used to identify the ‘’essential’’ double material 
topics. The threshold of 3 was chosen based on Vopak's judgement of the combined 
significance of the impacts, considering both the severity of impacts (scale, scope, 
irremediability) and their financial materiality.
Vopak deems essential topics as material, and till the next DMA, will issue a sustainability 
statement on these as per the relevant ESRS and Disclosure Requirements (DRs), 
prioritizing governance, management approach, policies, actions, and targets.

partners, Authorities & governmental organizations, Financial and capital markets, 
Neighbors and local communities, NGOs, Suppliers, and Employees (see table at the end 
of this note).

upstream (suppliers and contractors), own operations, and downstream (customers).

Affected stakeholders: We ensured the voices of affected stakeholders were 
considered on a topic-by-topic basis, especially where specific groups were more

Impact (I) Negative impact 
Vopak’s operations including chemical storage, handling, and vessel activities can lead to the emission of 
volatile organic compounds (VOCs). These compounds can lead to harmful impact on human health and the 
environment, contributing to ground-level ozone. These pollutants are known to cause respiratory issues and 
aggravate conditions like asthma.
Risk (R) Vopak faces significant climate transition and operational risks stemming from increasingly stringent 
regulations on Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) and hazardous emissions. To mitigate these risks, 
substantial capital investment in vapor recovery systems and advanced emission control technologies as 
internal floating roofs may be required.
Failure to effectively manage these emissions could result in untreated releases that harm surrounding 
communities, thereby jeopardizing our license to operate and exposing the company to fines or temporary 
facility closures.
Such disruptions pose a material threat to our financial performance and operational stability. Furthermore, 
an inability to meet evolving environmental standards may result in the loss of environment-conscious 
customers and restricted access to sustainability-focused capital markets, undermining Vopak’s long-term 
competitive position.
Opportunity (O) Lowering VOCs emissions with the help of high quality vapor management systems and similar solutions 
could result in a competitive advantage, considering the importance of this by customers and other 
stakeholders.
Management approach
Materiality, boundaries and reporting approach
In accordance with ESRS E2 (Pollution) and industry-specific standards, our DMA 
identifies air emissions, particularly VOCs, as a high-priority topic with negative impacts 
attributed to Vopak subsidiaries as well as operationally controlled JVs and associates. 
This is due to significant actual and perceived impact and financial implications.  We do not 
collect or report on upstream or downstream VOC emissions originating from our 
customers. Customers remain responsible for the regulatory reporting of their own 
emissions.
All data presented in this note covers subsidiaries, and operationally controlled JVs and 
associates.
We acknowledge the interaction of air emissions with other topics, such as process safety, 
greenhouse gas, and biodiversity and our assessment has considered these topics both 
individually and in the broader context. Please refer to General disclosures and materiality 
for the outcome of this assessment.
In line with the mapping to ESRS E2 - Pollution, this topic covers non-GHG air emissions. 
Therefore, the emissions and ecological impact of GHGs are not factored into this note; 
please refer instead to Note 2. Climate and energy in the sustainability statement.
Impact and screening
VOC emissions are deemed more significant than other air emissions for the following 
reasons:
Our operations, which include the storage and handling of products owned by our 
customers (oil, gas and chemicals), may result in the release of VOCs. 
For Vopak, emissions of VOCs are primarily attributed to the following major sources: 
  
Storage tanks: VOCs can escape from tanks storing volatile products, especially if the tanks are not 
adequately sealed or effectively vented. 
  
Loading and unloading operations: The transfer of products to and from vessels can lead to VOC 
emissions from spillage or leakage. 
  
Vessel operations: Vessels carrying volatile cargoes may release VOCs during loading, unloading, and 
transit, particularly in the absence of effective emission control measures.
•
Quantity: The total volume of VOC emissions is significantly higher than that of other air 
emissions, making their impact more pronounced.
•
Nature of operations: VOC emissions are directly linked to our core business activities, 
as they are released during the storage and handling of products at our facilities. In 
contrast, nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur oxides (SOx), and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) 
emissions result primarily from the combustion of fossil fuels, which is not central to our 
operations.
•
Substances of very high concern (SVHC): VOC emissions may contain high levels of 
SVHC and other substances of concern (SoC), further increasing their materiality.
•

These compounds can have harmful effects on both human health and the environment. 
It is crucial to understand that VOC emissions can come from a variety of sources within 
our operations, as explained in the Basis of calculation: VOC emission modeling.
Vopak recognizes the critical importance of minimizing our VOC footprint. Our first 
obligation is to comply fully with all local air quality regulations, though these may vary 
significantly across the jurisdictions we operate in. For example, while countries in the EU, 
various states in United States, and China have established stringent, government- 
mandated emission standards, in some jurisdictions, for instance in Southeast Asia, VOC 
emissions are not strictly regulated and often defer to businesses to implement VOC

Vopak's New Quantitative Dispersion Modeling for VOC Assessment: Shifting from 
Theoretical Impact to Exposure-Based Risk Analysis
Vopak has updated its VOC assessment approach to adopt a new quantitative dispersion 
methodology that is more representative of current asset configurations and operational 
activities. The current process utilizes detailed dispersion modeling based on worst-case 
operational scenarios, unlike the previous framework that relied on theoretical calculations 
of "polluted air volume" and broad assumptions. This updated approach reflects the 
specific chemical properties handled and the efficacy of installed mitigation measures 
such as IFRs, VRUs, and VTUs.
An enhancement in the process is the adoption of industry-standard thresholds to 
evaluate risk, replacing the previous method’s reliance on derived toxicity magnitudes and 
ecosystem likelihood factors, as further explained below.
Consequently, the representation of impact has shifted from a theoretical calculation of 
polluted air volume to a definitive assessment of concentration exposure. This 
methodology focuses on strict compliance with health & safety limits, where exceeding a 
threshold triggers immediate corrective action, instead of converting emissions into 
abstract societal values.

Dilemma: Reducing VOC emissions increases GHG emissions
To meet stringent air emission requirements, we are deploying VTUs across several sites 
to destroy harmful VOCs through thermal oxidation (combustion). The process of 
combusting VOCs fundamentally converts the carbon within these compounds into CO , a 
GHG. Furthermore, VTUs frequently require support gas (e.g., natural gas) to sustain the 
high temperatures necessary for complete destruction, adding significantly to our overall 
GHG footprint.
As the demands increase to treat VOCs, the use of VTUs is expected to rise in the future. 
We recognize this as a critical sustainability issue. We are actively exploring alternatives, 
including implementing more sustainable vapor handling methods, such as vapor recovery 
units (VRUs), that eliminate the need for combustion and support gas, allowing us to 
mitigate VOCs and prevent additional GHG emissions.
First layer - prevention: Prioritizing strategies that prevent vapor generation in the first 
place such as optimized tank design and vapor balancing system.
•
Second layer - reduction: Implementing operational measures to reduce emissions, 
including floating roofs to minimize vapor space and vapor return lines from loading 
platforms.
•
Third layer - treatment: Using vapor treatment technologies to further reduce 
emissions, such as flares, vapor treatment units (VTU), and residual thermal oxidizers 
(RTO).

Case study: Barge capture and control system at Vopak LA terminal
In alignment with the California Air Resources Board (CARB) at-berth regulations, 
Vopak’s Los Angeles terminal partnered with Clean Air Engineering – Maritime (CAEM) 
to commission the design, construction, and operation of two barge-based ship 
exhaust capture and treatment systems. The system’s capture device that collects the 
vessel exhaust is cleaned using catalyst embedded filters that simultaneously remove 
particulate matter and nitrogen oxides.
In 2025, the barges successfully serviced 48 tanker vessels, resulting in the direct 
removal of 0.2 metric tons of PM and 14.8 metric tons of NOx. This investment not only 
ensures full regulatory compliance for Vopak’s Southern California terminals, but also 
benefits the local community by reducing harmful air pollutants.

Governance, policies, and standards
Our GHG and sustainability policies encompass the same scope as our sustainability 
reporting scope, as described in General disclosures and materiality, ensuring 
comprehensive coverage and alignment. The responsibility for the implementation of these 
policies as well as group-wide coordination lies with the EVP of Global Operations and IT.
To encourage emissions reductions, we have implemented board-level remuneration 
policies aligned with our GHG reduction goals. Our GHG emissions reduction metric is part 
of the EB's short- and long-term incentive program and explained in detail in the 
Remuneration report.
We have a documented method for reporting emissions, which is consistent with the GHG 
Protocol and approved by the EB. This method takes into account both the operations and 
ownership of terminals and assets, enabling consistent reporting of Scope 1, 2, and 3 
emissions across subsidiaries, and JVs and associates. Vopak has developed accounting 
and reporting guidelines for energy consumption – a primary data source for calculating 
Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions – based on our internal reporting standards.
Vopak’s Scope 3 reporting manual covers the measurement, calculation, and reporting of 
Scope 3 CO₂ emissions . The document - periodically updated - follows the corresponding 
Corporate Value Chain Standard of the GHG Protocol and adheres to principles of 
relevance, completeness, consistency, transparency, and accuracy.
Vopak has developed a GHG emissions adjustment and restatement policy to ensure 
accurate, consistent, and transparent reporting aligned with the GHG Protocol. It includes 
rules regarding the recalculation of a Scope 1 and 2 base-year emissions in the case of 
significant changes including mergers, acquisitions, or divestments. Vopak documents and 
discloses any adjustments above the significant threshold (5% change) to accurately 
reflect its current operational footprint and organizational structure.
In previous reporting, we excluded offsetting from our medium- and long-term targets. 
We have since evolved this position. While our primary focus remains on directly reducing 
emissions through abatement (direct reduction), we acknowledge that high-quality, 
regulated offsetting may be necessary for residual emissions that we cannot eliminate 
within our operational boundaries or through available abatement options.

defined as a formal component of an organization’s strategy that details the specific 
actions, targets, and resources necessary to align the business with a sustainable, climate- 
neutral economy.
As specified in ESRS E1, this plan serves as a high-level framework demonstrating how a 
company’s business model and strategy are compatible with limiting global warming to 
1.5°C (in line with the Paris Agreement) and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.
As an independent infrastructure provider, Vopak fulfills a dual responsibility in this global 
energy evolution:

Vopak's transition plan is embedded in our daily operations and business strategy.

term value.

This integrated approach ensures that sustainability is not a separate initiative but a core 
element of how we run our business, driving responsible growth and long-term value

physical and transition risks and opportunities. Physical risks include both extreme short 
term weather events and long-term climate changes, covering aspects such as 
temperature, rainfall, flooding, wind, sea levels and fire. Transition risks and opportunities 
associated with the global shift towards a low-carbon economy cover aspects such as 
macroeconomic, political, technological, and market developments. Further details on our

Key decarbonization levers and financial support
To achieve our absolute GHG reduction target while accommodating emissions from our 
growth portfolio, we have an internal challenge to our BU’s to drive a deeper 60% 
reduction in Scope 1 and 2 by 2030. This creates the capacity to integrate new growth 
projects, which we also optimize for a low GHG footprint. These roadmaps outline the 
potential emissions reduction, as well as the opex and capex implications of each project.
The execution of projects, including those related to our decarbonization efforts, is 
internally managed through various programs, including the 3-Year Maintenance Program 
(3YMP) as well as locally managed capex initiatives. Progress against this program is 
measured quarterly and benchmarked against the original plan, as part of our BU reviews.
The implementation of the transition plan will necessitate both operating expenditure and 
capital expenditure commitments. Some initiatives, like renewable electricity, primarily 
involve opex, while others, such as energy efficiency measures, can actually generate 
opex savings. However, most projects necessitate capex investments. Significant cost 
components across the key levers of the transition plan have been identified in the section 
below.
Each project in our GHG reduction roadmap has undergone an analysis that weighs the 
potential reduction in emissions against the associated opex and capex, resulting in an 
estimated abatement cost. This abatement cost serves as a critical metric in investment 
decision-making, alongside other factors such as regulatory compliance, operational 
feasibility, technical viability, and resource availability. To guide decision making on these 
investments, we apply the shadow price of EUR 200 per tonne of CO e globally across all 
of our operational jurisdictions. This helps prioritize projects that deliver long-term 
sustainable value.
The following decarbonization levers enable our journey toward net-zero emissions:
Lever 1: Energy efficiency and replacement of fossil-fueled assets
Vopak has compiled a comprehensive fuel consuming assets inventory, identifying 
potential energy savings, and have determined that a major proportion of our GHG 
emissions can be mitigated by increasing the efficiency, electrification and replacement of 
our fossil-fueled assets. Our principle is to install electric and renewable-powered assets 
for both new installations and replacements, rather than gas- or diesel-fired options.
Furthermore, as vapor handling and treatment units can be highly emitting, we are 
continuously exploring ways to optimize, upgrade or replace gas-fired assets with the 
available alternatives. These include interventions and technologies such has Internal 
Floating Roofs (IFRs) and Regenerative Thermal Oxidizer (RTO).
Transitioning our "locked-in" assets - such as boilers, VTUs, and flares - to electric or 
renewable-powered alternatives will likely have significant capex impact. The precise 
financial implications will depend on the asset's location and type, as well as the resulting 
shift in opex for the new, electrically powered systems.
In 2025 we have allocated EUR 3.5 million of capex in our 3-Year-Maintenance Program 
for our decarbonization efforts.
Case study: E-boiler at Vopak Terminal Vlaardingen
Commissioned in March 2025, the new e-boiler at Vopak Terminal Vlaardingen has 
quickly demonstrated significant operational, environmental, and opex benefits. In its 
first six months, it produced 8 GWh of steam using carbon-free electricity, reducing our 
GHG footprint by 1,700 tonnes of CO , projecting an annual saving of 3,500 tonnes. 
Access to electricity day-ahead market participation and an opex subsidy ensured the 
project’s financial viability.
This success also highlights the substantial investment required for such meaningful 
decarbonization. The project represented a five-year, EUR 5 million commitment from 
initial concept to operation. This experience underscores that while targeting "low- 
hanging fruit" is an important first step, achieving our long-term climate-neutral goals 
will require a sustained commitment to these larger, more complex sustainability 
projects.
Case study: Energy assessment at Vopak terminals
In 2024, we initiated an energy assessment program targeting our highest energy- 
consuming terminals. By the end of 2025, assessments were completed for eleven of 
our top 25 energy-consuming terminals. This program focuses on increasing the 
efficiency of significant energy-consuming assets and assessing the potential for 
introducing new technologies. All identified improvements are integrated into each 
terminal's GHG reduction roadmap, with progress tracked during quarterly reviews. 
This program is a key driver for identifying energy reduction opportunities, which in 
turn directly reduces our CO  emissions.

Examples of initiatives identified and implemented include a reverse osmosis plant for a

Case study: Energy monitoring of Vopak terminals
In 2025, Vopak successfully piloted an in-house Energy Monitoring Tool (EMT) across 
its highest energy-consuming terminals. Built on the core philosophy that "you cannot 
reduce what you cannot measure," this application aggregates consumption data to 
assess and visualize operational trends, ranging from daily overviews to annual 
patterns.
The implementation of the EMT has improved energy management by providing 
actionable transparency. Before the tool's introduction, energy flows were often 
"invisible" to staff. Today, operational teams can track historical and daily consumption 
trends, allowing them to quickly identify specific opportunities to reduce waste.
To maximize the efficiency of these efforts, the tool utilizes strategic targeting. Rather 
than attempting to measure every data point, the EMT focuses on key identified areas 
within the terminal. This ensures that energy-saving initiatives are directed where they 
will yield the most significant impact.
Following the success of these initial pilots, Vopak is extending the application’s 
capabilities to the asset level. In 2026, the company aims to pilot asset-specific 
analytics - focusing on equipment such as pumps and boilers - to collect and analyze 
different operational parameters. This expansion will drive the next phase of the energy 
reduction journey, moving from terminal-wide overviews to granular, equipment-level 
efficiency.
Lever 2: Maximize the use of renewable electricity
We are transitioning all entities with market access to renewable electricity away from 
fossil-based sources. Many of our sites have successfully switched to renewable 
electricity to lower their Scope 2 GHG emissions, and we continue to explore opportunities 
in other countries. In 2025, we increased the share of renewable versus non-renewable 
electricity to 74% (2024: 69%). We purchase instruments, including Renewable Energy 
Certificates (RECs), each of which certifies that the bearer owns one megawatt-hour 
(MWh) of zero-carbon emissions electricity. 
Additionally, in some jurisdictions, we purchase Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for 
renewables, or electricity tariffs that incorporate use of renewable electricity. Through the 
purchase of those instruments, we reduce Scope 2 GHG emissions that arise from the use 
of grid electricity.
The cost of these instruments varies significantly based on geography, procurement 
method, and REC type. We analyze current renewable electricity instruments across our

Supply and demand imbalances: Changes in the renewable energy generation capacity 
(supply) or corporate/regulatory demand (e.g., new government mandates or corporate 
sustainability goals) can cause sudden price spikes or drops.
•
Regulatory changes: Policy shifts (e.g., removal of subsidies, creation of new 
compliance markets) can instantly re-price instruments. This is a major source of 
geopolitical risk.
•
Weather and seasonal variation: In certain markets, the supply of renewable generation 
(especially hydro or wind) is weather-dependent, leading to seasonal price volatility in

decoupled from the wholesale price of electricity, meaning a lower energy price does not 
guarantee a lower REC price.

Boilers: A steam boiler is a closed vessel that heats water to produce steam, which is 
then used for various applications at Vopak, mainly for heating of the products. Gas 
boilers use natural gas to heat the water, converting it into steam. Our boilers are critical 
to various operations at our terminals. Transitioning to low- or zero-carbon alternatives 
faces hurdles such as limited grid capacity for renewable electricity, the lack of suitable 
technologies, and the remaining lifespan of our existing boilers. However, we are 
confident that these challenges will not prevent us from achieving our GHG emission 
reduction targets.
•
Vapor treatment units: A VTU is a system designed to manage and process gaseous 
emissions that are released during the storage and handling of liquid products. Natural 
gas is used in a vapor treatment unit to generate enough heat to destroy the product 
particles. These emissions can originate from various sources within a terminal, including 
tanks, ships, trucks, loading racks, and jetties. The primary function of a VTU is to reduce 
emissions to comply with environmental regulations, ensure process safety, and maintain 
occupational health. VTUs are essential to reducing harmful VOC emissions and 
maintaining good air quality at many of our terminals. Combustion of VOCs involves a 
chemical reaction where these compounds, primarily composed of carbon and hydrogen 
(hydrocarbons) molecules, react with oxygen. During this reaction, the carbon atoms in 
the organic compound combine with oxygen from the air to form CO . CO  is an inherent 
and unavoidable product of their complete combustion. Besides this, the systems 
require support gas to achieve complete combustion of hazardous vapors, which 
increases our GHG emissions.

While these emissions are currently difficult to eliminate, we are constantly exploring

Transition plan and the progress on EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment
In 2025, we mapped our EU Taxonomy eligible activities with the decarbonization levers, 
identifying 14 activities across Climate Change Mitigation (CCM). Overall, we allocated 
EUR 6.2 million of capex and EUR 1.9 million of opex to CCM activities in 2025.

details, please see EU Taxonomy.
This is primarily due to the complexities associated with meeting the Do No Significant 
Harm (DNSH) criteria. Specifically, there are challenges in conducting comprehensive 
climate risk and vulnerability assessments under different climate scenarios (DNSH 
Appendix A) and environmental impact assessments for terminals located near sensitive 
biodiversity areas (DNSH Appendix D). These assessments are relevant to all identified 
eligible activities.
Consequently, we are currently unable to confirm that our activities fully align with the 
EU Taxonomy requirements. This also limits the ability to determine the precise impact of 
revenue, capex, opex, and future investment plans on the implementation of the 
company's transition plan.

Progress in implementing the announced transition plan
Progress across our three core decarbonization levers demonstrates notable results

The increasing use of renewable electricity (Lever 2) has contributed to a reduction of our

Simultaneously, the Energy Efficiency and Fossil-Fueled Asset Replacement lever (Lever 1)

mitigation of Scope 1 GHG emissions.  Our total Scope 1 emissions have reduced from

While the first two levers track the abatement of existing emissions, progress under Lever 
3: Reduce the emissions of our growth, relates to avoided emissions rather than reported 
reductions. This lever ensures that all new projects, such as a new terminal, are designed 
with low-carbon alternatives, like electric boilers over gas-fired options, from the outset. 
Because these measures prevent new emission sources before the commissioning of a 
project, the resulting emission savings do not appear in our emissions reporting; these are 
preventative actions that future-proof our growth trajectory from an environmental 
perspective.
