Scope 3 emissions
The Scope 3 emissions in 2025 were primarily attributed to the purchase of goods and 
services, construction and maintenance projects, investments, and waste generated by 
our operations.
Vopak has not yet set a Scope 3 emissions target in order to allow more time to improve 
data quality and procurement processes for accurately measuring progress. 
Beyond administrative hurdles, we face operational challenges in mitigating emissions, 
particularly due to the scarcity of low-carbon materials for our strategic growth projects. 
Further details are provided under Target Setting and Mitigation below. We aim to report 
on our action plan to address Scope 3 emissions in our next Annual Report.
Methodology and categorization
Vopak calculates its Scope 3 inventory in accordance with the GHG Protocol Corporate 
Standard (2004) and the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard (2011). The reporting period 
aligns with the calendar year, covering all entities under Vopak’s operational control.
In alignment with the GHG Protocol, we review all 15 Scope 3 categories to determine their 
relevance and materiality to our operations. Based on this review, we identify that the 
categories related to the movement and lifecycle of physical products sold (Categories 4, 
9, 10, 11, and 12) and leased assets or franchises (Categories 8, 13, and 14) do not apply to 
our specific business activities.
Specifically, Category 11 (Use of Sold Products) is excluded because Vopak’s core 
operations are limited to storage and handling services. As we do not take ownership of 
the fossil fuels, gases, or chemicals we manage, we have no control over their ultimate 
use. Consequently, Category 11 falls outside our value chain boundaries.
Consequently, our Scope 3 reporting focuses on the following relevant upstream and 
investment-based activities:
1. Purchased goods and services (Category 1)
2. Capital goods (Category 2)
Capital goods reporting is divided into two distinct sub-categories to reflect the different 
drivers of emissions:
2
Scope: Includes all global operational expenditures (opex) booked during the reporting 
year.
•
Methodology: Vopak employs a spend-based method, utilizing the UK Department for 
Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) database for sector-specific emission 
factors.
•
Data processing: Specific emission factors are allocated to the top 90% of spend, while 
the remaining 10% is estimated using weighted averages of parent categories.
•
To ensure accuracy across different markets, emissions are adjusted by a purchasing 
power factor based on the terminal's country and corrected for inflation where 
necessary.
•
Growth - Major Projects (Cat 2.1): This covers major projects exceeding €10 million that 
reached Ready-for-Operations (RFO) status during the year.

Calculation: A hybrid approach is used. Primary materials (steel and concrete) are 
calculated based on actual quantities (activity-based), labor emissions are calculated 
through an extrapolation method which applies a fixed 10% markup to a project’s total 
material and utility footprint to more accurately reflect the physical reality of labor 
emissions across different wage regions compared to spend-based calculations.
•
Sustaining capex (Cat 2.2): Covers all other global capital expenditures excluding 
growth projects.

Limitations
Vopak is committed to continuously improving its reporting approach to ensure the

In 2025, Vopak reported 417,313 metric tons of Scope 3 GHG emissions. The emissions 
were primarily attributed to the purchase of goods and services, construction and 
maintenance projects, investments, and waste generated by our operations. We updated 
several calculation methodologies this year to ensure our reporting matures and stays 
aligned with international standards. Major variations between years are caused by

impacts. This limits year-on-year comparability.
Major changes to the 2025 data are attributed to the following:
Target setting and mitigation
While we have made significant progress in reducing our Scope 1 and 2 emissions, tackling 
Scope 3 presents unique challenges. We are committed to reporting our footprint, but we 
currently face structural dilemmas that complicate the setting of absolute Scope 3 
emission reduction targets.
Given these evolving boundaries and data limitations, we believe setting an absolute 
emissions reduction target for Scope 3 at this stage would be premature. In 2025, we 
initiated an assessment to investigate mitigation options within our Scope 3 emissions. 
The primary objective of that assessment is to create a roadmap that first identifies the 
foundational changes necessary to set credible targets, such as improving data quality and 
procurement processes. Second, the project will evaluate potential mitigation measures 
and abatement efforts from a financial and resource perspective. We are currently in the 
final stages of this analysis and expect to disclose the outcomes in our 2026 Annual 
Report.
Fuel- and energy-related activities: We advanced our reporting approach for 
renewable electricity to better align with the GHG Protocol. This updated methodology 
factors in transmission and distribution losses as the primary factor for renewable 
electricity. By excluding upstream production emissions for purchased renewable 
electricity, we provide a more accurate reflection of our footprint.
•
Capital goods: We transitioned from a spend-based factor to a material-intensity 
extrapolation method for the working hours in construction projects. This change 
corrects purchasing power distortions where regional labor cost variations previously 
inflated carbon footprint data. While we commissioned several tank and terminal projects 
in 2025, these assets had a smaller collective GHG footprint than those completed in 
2024.
•
Waste generated in operations: We improved our accounting for waste by adopting 
specific emission factors from the Netherlands Emission Authority (NEA) for select 
categories. We continue to use DEFRA factors for remaining categories to maintain a 
reliable overview of our environmental impact from greenhouse gas emissions.
•
Our growth strategy involves building the infrastructure of the future. Whether we are 
constructing storage for low-carbon fuels or retrofitting assets for hydrogen, these 
projects require materials such as steel and concrete. This creates a paradox: to 
transition toward a sustainable future, we must invest in construction today, which 
inevitably causes spikes in our Category 2 (Capital goods) emissions. For example, in 
years when we undertake large-scale projects to support our strategy, our Scope 3 
emissions will naturally increase.
•
A significant portion of our Scope 3 calculation currently relies on spend-based 
methodologies, in which we estimate emissions based on the financial value of goods 
purchased. We must use this approach when primary data is unavailable. However, this 
creates a distortion: economic factors, such as inflation or market price spikes, can 
artificially increase our reported emissions, even if the actual carbon content remains 
constant. Under this method, purchasing more sustainable goods does not necessarily 
result in a lower reported footprint, as these goods are often more expensive.
•
Our procurement is geographically distributed to support our global operations and  
involves thousands of suppliers worldwide. This diversity presents two distinct 
challenges:
•
Limited influence: Many of our vendors consider Vopak to be a comparatively small 
customer. This limits our commercial leverage to mandate specific carbon reporting 
standards or drive rapid decarbonization in their operations.
•
Regional maturity: We operate globally and purchase locally in markets with varying 
levels of sustainability maturity. In regions where Scope 3 reporting is not yet a 
regulatory priority or cultural norm, obtaining high-quality primary data from local 
suppliers remains a significant hurdle.
•
The market reality for green steel and concrete remained challenging in 2025. 
The commercial availability of genuine low-carbon materials is currently scarce, and 
where these materials are available, they command a significant "green premium."

Energy use
Introduction
Our reporting on energy use includes the combustion of fossil fuels (Scope 1) and 
purchased utilities (Scope 2), namely electricity and steam.
In the chemical and oil storage terminals, fossil fuels are primarily used for product heating 
and vapor handling & treatment purposes and electricity is primarily used for powering the 
pumps for the movement of products.
The magnitude of the energy consumption at Vopak terminals depends on:
For gas (non-LNG) storage terminals, electricity is the most significant energy carrier as it 
drives the boil-off gas systems to liquefy the vapors that arise from storing and 
transporting liquid gases. While electricity is also consumed for pumping and heating 
activities, fossil fuel is consumed for emergency flare systems.
For LNG storage terminals, seawater used for regasification is the biggest energy carrier. 
Regasification is the process through which the LNG is transformed back into gaseous 
natural gas. It requires a large amount of energy that can be extracted from seawater using 
a heat exchanger. The cooled seawater is returned to the sea. Other energy carriers 
include natural gas for vapor handling and treatment purposes and electricity for vapor 
compression and pumping activities.

Our strategy
We are dedicated to delivering safe, reliable, and efficient storage of essential products for 
everyday life to help the world flow forward. Whilst traditional products are an important 
part of our current business, Vopak embraces the energy and feedstock transition towards 
low-carbon products and services. This is key to continue fulfilling our purpose and 
ensuring alignment with the changing world. We believe that the world needs to pursue 
the dual objectives of limiting climate change while providing access to secure, affordable, 
and sustainable energy and feedstocks for all.
As communicated during the Capital Markets Day on March 13, 2025, we aim to grow our 
gas and industrial footprint by investing EUR 2.6 billion by 2030, while we also re- 
confirmed our ambition to invest EUR 1.4 billion in energy transition infrastructure.
We measure the attainment of our EUR 2.6 billion and EUR 1.4 billion ambitions through a 
comprehensive assessment of our ongoing proportional investments and financial 
commitments. This approach ensures that for JVs, associates, and subsidiaries, the capex 
investments and commitments are determined by multiplying the relevant measure by the 
Vopak economic rights (in the majority of cases determined by the legal ownership 
percentage). From 2022 until the end of 2025, we have invested or committed 
EUR 1,656 million (of which EUR 1,076 million under construction and EUR 580 million 
commissioned) in growing the base in industrial and gas projects and EUR 256 million (of 
which EUR 191 million under construction and EUR 65 commissioned) in the acceleration 
towards new energies and sustainable feedstocks.
Contributing to the acceleration of the energy and feedstock transition is a crucial part of 
our corporate strategy, updated frequently. It's crucial to understand the dynamics of the 
energy and feedstock transition, where, how, and when it's unfolding. As such, we monitor 
the evolving energy landscape, traditional and new sources alike - across sectors, 
products, and regions, mapping both current and projected use. As the speed of transition 
is to a large extent also driven by regulatory measures, Vopak is keeping track of 
developments in the relevant regulatory framework with announcements by countries 
(e.g., Inflation Reduction Act in the US), regions (e.g., Emissions Trading System and 
Renewable Energy Directive III in the EU), and industry bodies (e.g., International Maritime 
Organization and International Air Transport Association).
As the world moves toward a more sustainable future, our talented workforce is at the 
forefront, fostering partnerships that drive the development of infrastructure solutions for 
new energies.
Governance and policies
Executive Vice President Global Business Development and his team coordinate Vopak’s 
existing prospective portfolio of energy transition infrastructure investments. They inform 
the EB and SB on the progress and development in this area through reporting on a regular 
basis. Although a variety of data elements are included, the main metrics used to monitor 
the progress on these strategic pillars are the estimated capital expenditures spent and 
the returns for the projects in the identification, selection, and definition phase, and their 
expected final investment decision date, as well as the projects in the execution phase. 
For the projects that have been commissioned, we monitor their performance compared to 
the original business case. The report provides insight into the current achievement of the 
externally disclosed ambition (EUR 2.6 billion proportional investments in Grow and EUR 
1.4 billion proportional investments in Accelerate in the period up to 2030), of the mid-term 
proportional capex targets, which are part of the LTIP Plans for senior management, and 
the long-term outlook.
Investment Policy
The Investment Policy serves as the framework for aligning capital allocation with Vopak’s 
strategy, specifically targeting portfolio performance improvement, growth in industrial and 
gas terminals, and the acceleration toward energy transition infrastructure. Investment 
proposals are rigorously screened to ensure they strictly adhere to our Sustainability 
Roadmap and Code of Conduct, balancing societal and environmental responsibilities with 
economic value creation. Financial discipline is maintained by categorizing projects into 
brownfield expansions, and greenfield developments, which focus on long-term option 
value; however, all investments are required to exceed the applicable Weighted Average 
Cost of Capital (WACC) to ensure the enhancement of shareholder value.
To guarantee transparent governance and disciplined execution, all projects follow the 
Vopak Project Management (VPM) procedure and strict approval thresholds outlined in the 
Management Authorization Policy (MAP), requiring Executive or Supervisory Board 
validation for significant commitments. The policy integrates comprehensive risk 
mitigation, including a Foreign Exchange (FX) Risk Management Policy to protect capital 
expenditures against currency fluctuations. Furthermore, the company maintains a robust 
reporting cycle where project status and long-term financial scenarios - specifically 
monitoring Net Debt to EBITDA - are updated quarterly to ensure continuous strategic 
alignment and financial transparency.

Our strategy to facilitate the energy transition is centered on a significant shift in our 
portfolio toward cleaner fuels, whilst growing our existing activities. This involves 
developing infrastructure solutions for new energies and sustainable fuels and feedstocks 
across four focus areas: clean hydrogen (blue and green), infrastructure for carbon capture 
use/storage (CCU/S), battery solutions (e.g., BESS), and low-carbon fuels and feedstock 
(e.g., biodiesel, green methanol, and chemical recycling).

EU Taxonomy
Introduction
EU Regulation 2020/852, commonly referred to as the EU Taxonomy, constitutes one of 
the cornerstones for both the European Green Deal as well as the EU Action Plan on 
Sustainable Finance. Its ultimate goal is to help shift capital flows towards more 
sustainable investments. To do so, it provides clear guidance on what activities can be 
deemed “environmentally sustainable”. The EU Taxonomy is a transparency tool that has 
introduced mandatory disclosure obligations for non-financial undertakings such as Vopak.
As from 2026, Vopak has integrated its EU Taxonomy disclosures directly into this 
sustainability statement to ensure that our environmental transition KPIs are presented 
alongside our material reporting requirements.
For an economic activity to be identified as environmentally sustainable, it must contribute 
to the achievement of at least one of the following six environmental objectives:
For each of these environmental objectives, the EU Taxonomy defines a list of economic 
activities that could potentially contribute to achieving such objectives. These activities 
are listed in dedicated Delegated Acts:
The EU Taxonomy can be considered a “living document” that may be expanded to include 
additional activities and sectors of the economy, as part of the future publication of further 
Delegated Acts or amendments. This will imply that companies subject to the Regulation, 
such as Vopak, will have to adapt to possible future changes, and all the FAQs available up 
until this day.
Reporting requirements 2025
Vopak, subject to EU Regulation 2020/852, is required to comply with the EU Taxonomy 
Regulation, and disclose the following:
Taxonomy-eligibility and Taxonomy-alignment for all environmental objectives, namely 
CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, and BIO.
In the context of compliance with the Transition Plan under CSRD (ESRS E1-16e), 
Taxonomy-aligned KPIs shall be disclosed as evidence supporting the implementation of 
the transition plan and conditionally, Taxonomy-eligible KPIs are also allowed and will be 
presented in the tables below.
Vopak's EU Taxonomy approach
Description of the approach for determining Taxonomy-eligibility
Vopak has conducted an assessment of eligible activities against the six objectives, 
including all non-turnover related activities, as well as an adjustment of the calculation of 
the opex KPI.
The outcome of the assessment is the identification of 24 Taxonomy-eligible activities.
The main steps of the Taxonomy-eligibility assessment process are as follows.
Step 1: Short list of potentially Taxonomy-eligible activities
We carefully assessed all economic activities listed in the Taxonomy, covering both 
turnover-related and non-turnover-related activities as specified in the Delegated Acts. 
This involved examining each activity separately to create an initial list of our eligible 
taxonomy activities for all environmental objectives, complete with their descriptions.
Objective 1: Climate change mitigation (CCM)•
Objective 2: Climate change adaptation (CCA)•
Objective 3: Sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources (WTR)•
Objective 4: Transition to a circular economy (CE)•
Objective 5: Pollution prevention and control (PPC)•
Objective 6: Protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO)•
The “Climate Delegated Act” (Commission Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 of 4 June 
2021), which includes activities related to the climate change mitigation (CCM) and the 
climate change adaptation (CCA) objectives. An “Amendment of the Climate Delegated 
Act” has been published in the Official Journal in November 2023 (Commission 
Delegated Regulation 2023/2485 of 27 June 2023); such amendment includes additional 
activities related to the climate change mitigation (CCM) and the climate change 
adaptation (CCA) objectives and introduces some changes for existing activities.

Basis of preparation and reporting scope
Note on integrated reporting (EU Taxonomy and ESRS): In accordance with the CSRD 
and ESRS 1, the EU Taxonomy disclosures are now integrated directly into our 
Sustainability Statement. This integration reflects the regulatory requirement to 
consolidate all sustainability-related financial and impact data into a single and audited 
report. By presenting our Taxonomy-eligible and KPIs (turnover, capex, and opex) 
alongside our topical climate disclosures, we provide stakeholders with a transparent view 
of how our capital allocation supports the European Green Deal and our long-term 
transition objectives.
IFRS 10 and equity method: The EU Taxonomy includes reporting of entities that are 
consolidated in the Group’s Financial Statements in line with the requirements of IFRS 10. 
As such, the EU Taxonomy reporting scope is limited to subsidiaries.
IAS 28 and investment proportionate KPIs: The Taxonomy gives non-financial 
undertakings the option to voluntarily disclose additional KPIs based on turnover, capex, 
and opex that include investments in equity accounted JVs and associates, pursuant to 
IFRS 11 or IAS 28, on a pro-rata basis corresponding to their share in the equity.
Vopak has voluntarily made use of this option in its previous disclosures, by disclosing 
separate tables for each of the indicators. In 2025, Vopak has decided to discontinue this 
disclosure in order to streamline its EU Taxonomy reporting.

Management approach
Materiality, reporting approach and boundaries
Our DMA identifies Process safety and the prevention of spills as a material topic from 
both an impact and financial perspective. In accordance with ESRS E2 (Pollution) and 
industry-specific standards, our assessment identifies material IROs across all subsidiaries 
as well as JVs and associates under our operational control.
Accordingly, the required reporting scope for process safety is broader than our financial 
statements, ensuring the consistent application of our mitigation and prevention standards 
across our defined operational boundary. 
This ensures that process safety risks and impacts are managed uniformly across all 
entities where we have the authority to implement safety protocols.
All data presented in this note covers subsidiaries and operationally controlled JVs & 
associates.
Impact and screening
Process safety is fundamental to our license to operate. The primary impacts associated 
with this material topic stem from incidents involving Loss of Primary Containment (LOPC), 
product contamination, damage to installations, and fire. Failure to manage these risks 
effectively could lead to catastrophic consequences, including loss of life and severe 
impact on surrounding communities. Beyond the human and environmental toll, such 
events pose significant commercial risks, including the severance of customer 
relationships and substantial financial liabilities.
Conversely, by prioritizing process safety and spill prevention, we enhance our market 
position. Effective management reduces operational costs by minimizing equipment 
damage and waste while demonstrating a steadfast commitment to environmental 
responsibility.
Effective handling of stored products is underpinned by rigorous documentation and 
proactive risk mitigation. We require customers to provide Safety Data Sheets (SDS), which 
are cataloged globally and used to create product-specific safety information cards. These 
cards are integrated directly into our daily work instructions to guarantee safe handling at 
the operational level.
Our safety management follows a systematic cycle from mandatory reporting to 
company-wide learning. All personnel are required to track process safety incidents 
through a centralized reporting and action system.
Every reported incident undergoes a formal evaluation and investigation guided by our 
global standards. By performing regular monitoring and root cause analysis, we implement 
corrective measures to prevent recurrence. Furthermore, we foster a culture of continuous 
improvement by communicating "major incident learnings" across all global facilities 
through standardized safety alerts.

Internal audit and asset integrity
In 2024, we finalized the multi-year cycle of our internal audit program Terminal Health 
Assessment (THA) 2.0, in line with the Chemical Distribution Institute - Terminal (CDI-T) 
requirements and industry best practice. It is a key governance tool within Vopak’s 
integrated management system, providing the leadership with the assurance that terminals 
are implementing and maintaining their assets, processes, procedures, and knowledge 
following the legal regulations, Vopak standards, and best practices. In 2025, we have 
taken the learnings from the THA 2.0 audit program and relaunched integrated Terminal 
Risk Control Assessments (TRCAs). In total, during 2025, we audited a total of 3 terminals 
in the pilot stage. Findings of the audits are registered, followed up, and tracked in our 
reporting and action tracking system.
In parallel, the 3-Year Maintenance Program (3YMP) plays a critical role in ensuring asset 
integrity. This risk-based approach evaluates the maintenance needs of key assets, such 
as tanks, pipelines, and control systems, balancing the priorities against routine 
maintenance activities. The program is reviewed annually during the budget cycle, with 
progress tracked monthly against initial plans during BU reviews. If additional maintenance 
needs arise, these are carefully assessed and resourced to maintain safety.
Incident classification and reporting
Process incidents are classified into three primary categories: process safety, 
environmental, and asset damage. To standardize severity reporting, process safety 
events are categorized using a tiered system. Tier 1 represents high-impact or 
catastrophic incidents, while Tier 2 includes moderately significant events. Tier 1 and Tier 
2 incidents are reported externally while lower-tier events are documented and managed 
internally for continuous improvement.
The total number of Tier 1 and Tier 2 incidents per 200,000 hours worked are reported as 
the Process Safety Event Rate (PSER).
Besides the Tier 1 and 2 reporting, we also report all uncontained and contained spills to 
the environment exceeding 200 kg released, irrespective of their tier classification, 
including details on location, quantity, and the substance involved.
Spills to water are reported universally, while damages (product contaminations and asset 
damages) are only included if they exceed EUR 50,000 per event.
To maintain accountability, all Tier 1 and Tier 2 incidents are reported to the EB within 24 
hours.
Governance, policies, and standards
To maintain high safety standards across our international network, Vopak utilizes a robust 
governance framework known as the Vopak Integrated Management System (VIMS). This 
integrated system combines global standards, blueprint processes, and leadership 
behaviors to ensure consistency and excellence.
In alignment with international best practices, we report process safety according to API 
RP 754. This standard classifies events by significance, with Tier 1 representing the most

can cause enduring erosion of brand equity and stakeholder trust, complicating recruitment, retention, and

Opportunity (O) Adhering to our commitment to our health and safety standards can significantly reduce incident rates, which 
in turn can minimize risks related to our reputation, as well as decrease costs associated with compensation,

Management approach
Materiality, reporting approach and boundaries
Our DMA identifies Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) as a material topic from both an 
impact and financial perspective. The assessment confirms that OHS carries significant 
actual and potential negative impacts as well as risks across our operational footprint, 
involving direct employees, contracted workers and personnel within operationally 
controlled JVs and associates.
Consequently, we have implemented robust mitigation measures designed to safeguard 
the physical and mental well-being of all workers, ensuring our safety standards are 
applied consistently regardless of employment type or entity structure.
To remain compliant with ESRS 1 requirements regarding the reporting boundary, we have 
disclosed key performance indicator data for financially controlled entities, including the 
split between own workers and value chain workers.  In addition, we have disclosed entity 
specific data, which includes subsidiaries and operationally controlled JVs and 
associates.  For details on how we classify our own workforce and value chain workers, 
please refer to Key changes in the preparation of sustainability information in General 
disclosures and materiality.
Impact and screening
For all OHS risks, the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) process of managing risks is applied 
within Vopak’s Integrated Management standard.
Each terminal identifies potential hazards at its location by assessing both standard and 
non-standard activities performed on-site, as well as the associated products handled. 
These risks are assessed, including identifying those who may be impacted, and control 
measures are applied using the control hierarchy and the “as low as reasonably 
practicable” (ALARP) principle. The manner in which the risk assessments are conducted is 
based on international best practices including the Occupational Safety & Health 
Administration (OSHA), the American Petroleum Institute (API), the International 
Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP), and relevant guidelines of the International 
Standards Organization (ISO) among others. The risks and applicable controls are 
monitored for effectiveness, either through internal checks or through specialist third- 
party testing and/or surveys as required by legislation, standards, and procedures. The 
output is in the form of identification and implementation of corrective actions and 
improvements.
128 Vopak Annual Report 2025 Sustainability notes

The main risks we have identified for our own workforce and value chain workers, in 
particular operational staff, include injuries and fatalities due to an isolated, on-site 
incident. This could include falls from heights or injuries from a Loss of Primary 
Containment (LOPC) event, which may result in acute exposure to potentially harmful 
products or injury. Some risks are not related to an incident, but are still present in 
day-to-day activities. An example is the risk of long-term exposure and injury from 
hazards, such as normal product handling or noise exposure. Both types of risk are 
managed through our OHS management program.
Furthermore, on-site value chain workers, who perform tasks such as maintenance on 
verified clean equipment or work on new construction projects in which products have not 
yet been handled, are generally less exposed to product-related risks. Their primary risks 
involve falls from heights, impact injuries from equipment handling, poor ergonomics, and 
general slip and trip hazards.
The PDCA process requires input from many different people at various stages. To assess 
risks, we bring together teams with a variety of skills and experience. These teams might 
include subject-matter experts and those who work directly in the value chain. Regular 
awareness training and engagement activities, such as toolbox talks, lessons learned 
sharing, and general risk mitigation discussions, involve value chain workers to assess and 
implement controls. In addition, there are formal meetings where safety, health, and 
environmental (SHE) matters are addressed, involving both SHE committees and 
management teams, where active participation is required to receive feedback from the 
organization on specific SHE topics.
Governance, policies, procedures, and standards
Vopak operates a global terminal network handling liquid and gaseous products. If handled 
incorrectly, these products can endanger our workforce, value chain workers, and local 
communities. Furthermore, certain onsite activities, such as construction, can also pose 
dangers to people, although these risks are not directly induced by the products we store. 
We mitigate these inherent risks by storing and handling our products with care, adhering 
to the latest safety standards, best practices, and applicable legislation.
All our terminals are expected to adhere to the highest safety and operational standards, 
complying with both local legal requirements and Vopak's rigorous internal standards, 
always applying the stricter of the two. Each terminal has implemented an OHS 
management system aligned with these standards to ensure effective local risk 
management.
Vopak is committed to a strong safety culture that promotes continuous learning and 
psychological safety, an environment where all individuals feel empowered to contribute 
and raise concerns without fear of reprisal. This culture is driven by dedicated leadership 
at each terminal, empowering individuals to take responsibility for their own safety and 
that of their colleagues, and is supported by BU and global organizational structures.
Global and BU SHE Leadership meet monthly to address safety performance, discuss 
targets and share best practices. Key topics in 2025 included the launch of the new 
Terminal Risk Control Assessment (TRCA) audit program with Global Internal Audit; 
incident management and learning improvements; safety leadership culture development; 
and SHE system improvements (including Management of Change (MOC), aligning with the 
Systematic Cause Analysis Technique (SCAT) model, and system efficiencies).
Safety is a shared leadership responsibility, with functional oversight by the Chief Financial 
Officer (CFO). Global safety performance is reported monthly to the EB and Strategic 
Committee, supplemented by quarterly performance reviews and ad-hoc updates on key 
incidents.
Vopak manages occupational workplace risks by identifying and assessing hazards, 
implementing controls, and monitoring their effectiveness through an occupational health 
program aligned with legal standards. We also support employee well-being through 
initiatives such as health checks, dietary guidance, and programs promoting mental well- 
being and work-life balance.
Vopak Integrated Management Systems (VIMS) and standards cover key design, 
construction, personal and process safety, as well as operational and maintenance 
processes. Vopak has also developed the “Fundamentals on Safety”, a standard based on 
the highest-risk activities on our terminals that could result in catastrophic incidents. 
Adherence to these eight fundamentals is non-negotiable for everyone who works on our 
sites.
Routine and non-routine terminal activities are managed through our control of work 
standards. All Vopak’s own workforce and value chain workers are required to adhere to 
our SHE policies and standards. These requirements are formalized in contracts and 
supported by mandatory training and procedures at all locations. The responsibility for the 
implementation of these policies and standards lies with our EVP of Global Operations and 
IT.

Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels
At Vopak, we believe that everyone working at our sites should return home safely. 
However, incidents do occur. All OHS incidents are managed on-site through each 
terminal’s emergency response plan, with escalation depending on the severity of the 
event, in accordance with Vopak's standards for emergency response, crisis management, 
business continuity, and local legal requirements.
The immediate response to an incident is to protect the lives of the people on site, mitigate 
the consequences, and prevent further escalation of the event. Medical treatment is 
provided as needed for those affected by the incident.
Each location is responsible for providing the necessary medical and psychological support 
following an occupational injury or illness, including compensation or financial coverage for 
long-term disability or serious injury. This support is usually facilitated through mandatory 
insurance in accordance with local regulations. Long-term support and reintegration, 
including return-to-work initiatives, are arranged in accordance with terminal/BU 
procedures and legal requirements.
With the aim of being a learning organization, Vopak learns from its incidents, including 
high-potential near misses. We have identified incidents that require TRIPOD method 
investigation, root cause/Tripod lite and, where it can provide useful insights, a human 
factor analysis. The learnings are shared throughout the organization in different formats 
and, where required, procedures and standards are adjusted.

Vopak Code of Conduct
To fulfill our role in society, we consider it vital that employees, contractors, suppliers, 
customers, and JV partners understand and share our Vopak Values. Our Vopak Values 
define the culture and behaviors that we are committed to embedding throughout Vopak 
(e.g., Care for Safety, Health & Environment, Integrity, Team Spirit, Commitment, and 
Agility). It covers various topics, including anti-bribery and anti-corruption, honest business 
conduct, conflicts of interest, health & safety, and human rights.
The Vopak Code of Conduct serves as a comprehensive guide, offering context and 
elaboration of Vopak Values. It applies to all Vopak employees globally, including 
temporary staff. Emphasis is placed on managers for ethical guidance, and the EB commits 
to non-retaliation for Code of Conduct reporting. The Code of Conduct aims to provide 
clarity on expected behavior, ethical decision-making, and reputation safeguarding. 
Vopak’s Code of Conduct forbids gifts to political parties or religious groups. The Code of 
Conduct also strictly limits gifts and entertainment. The functions that have the highest 
likelihood of being exposed to corruption and bribery are Procurement and Maintenance, 
together making up approximately 14% of the workforce. Furthermore, the Code of 
Conduct states that “When dealing with governments or other governmental agencies, 
Vopak companies are encouraged to promote and defend their legitimate business 
objectives, within the limits set by this Code of Conduct. They may do so directly or 
through bodies such as trade associations.”

Vopak Speak Up Policy
Our Speak Up platform provides employees, value chain workers, and other stakeholders a 
secure channel to raise concerns regarding Code of Conduct compliance, including alleged 
human and labor rights violations. 
Our dedicated investigation team follows an investigation protocol that adheres to strict 
principles of confidentiality, respect for anonymity, non-retaliation, objectivity, and the 
right to be heard. Anyone who believes they have been retaliated against for raising a 
good faith concern can also report such retaliation, which will be investigated as a 
potential Code of Conduct violation. Vopak is subject to legal requirements under national 
law transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1937 with regard to the protection of whistleblowers.  
Our ambition is to have zero breaches of the Code of Conduct.
Vopak has implemented a third-party Speak Up software system. This system is 
communicated and made available throughout the company to report ethical concerns or 
dilemmas. Once logged, the system provides a workflow application that ensures that 
reports are categorized, allocated to a case handler, monitored, and followed up. All 
employees, value chain workers, and other stakeholders can report their concerns through 
this system and are encouraged to use it as part of Vopak’s speak up culture. The tracking 
and monitoring of individual Speak Up reports, including the closing of actions, is done 
through the system.
Vopak conducts an annual survey among a selection of employees to assess whether our 
employees are aware of, and trust, the Speak Up system and the channels provided. When 
appropriate, Vopak takes measures in response to the survey outcome.
Where applicable, Global Internal Audit (GIA) assesses whether the recommended remedy 
has been effective within months of the completion of the investigation. It also monitors 
and responds to any trends identified in investigations. The number of reports and the 
status are reported quarterly to the EB and Audit Committee.

Societal and environmental criteria for the selection of suppliers
Through pre-qualification and tactical procurement stages (i.e., specification of needs, 
contractor/supplier selection, and contracting of contractor/supplier), Vopak aims to work 
only with contractors and suppliers who meet the societal and environmental criteria that 
match the work to be performed. Qualification is performed in a two-step approach. The 
first step is screening suppliers on generic requirements such as legal structure, financial 
situation, relevant certification (ISO), anti-bribery, legal proceedings, plans to prevent 
forced labor, misconduct, etc.
In the next step, suppliers are screened on work-specific requirements such as HSE 
records, International Labour Organization (ILO) compliance, sanction compliance, 
technical requirements, Quality Assurance (QA), relevant experience, specific human rights 
plans, and cybersecurity action plans. During execution of the work, the Contractor and 
Supplier Performance Management Process (C&SPM) sets out a comprehensive and 
systematic approach to managing the performance and relationships of new and existing 
contractors and suppliers over time to monitor and continuously improve performance.
For details on the outcome of supplier screening and the process, please refer to the 
Human rights and decent work section of Non-material ESG information.
Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
At Vopak, we are committed to conducting our business fairly, transparently, and with 
integrity, applying the highest ethical and legal standards. We do not make, offer, or 
authorize bribes, nor do we condone any other form of unethical business practice. Our 
rules and procedures related to anti-corruption or anti-bribery are set out in our Anti- 
Bribery & Corruption (ABC) Policy, which is accessible to our employees. This policy is 
consistent with the United Nations Convention against Corruption.
Similarly, Vopak has a Fraud Risk Management policy. This policy provides practical 
guidance to embed a periodic assessment of fraud risks, the development thereof as well 
as defining mitigation action to improve fraud prevention controls. It also provides 
guidance on how to proceed if a suspected fraud is identified or reported.
The BUs are required to perform annual bottom-up fraud risk assessments as part of their 
enterprise risk management process. All employees are expected to complete mandatory 
training on anti-corruption and anti-bribery every other year. Any alleged violation of our 
anti-corruption or anti-bribery rules and procedures can be reported through our Speak Up 
platform (as previously described) and is then investigated by an independent team.

Strategic stakeholder engagement, memberships, and lobbying
Vopak is committed to responsible and constructive engagement in the communities in 
which it operates. The company places strong emphasis on building and sustaining 
meaningful relationships with its stakeholders, with particular attention to local 
communities. From the early phases of a project through the full operational life of our 
terminals, Vopak engages proactively with stakeholders to identify, understand, and 
address relevant topics and concerns. Depending on the stakeholder group and the 
subject matter, engagement takes place through a range of channels, including in-person 
meetings, written communication, company websites, social media, open days, site visits, 
and participation in public consultations.
An annual review of stakeholder engagement activities is conducted to confirm alignment 
with Vopak’s policies, culture, Code of Conduct, sustainability policy, purpose, and 
business strategy. As part of this review, a questionnaire is distributed each year to 
members of StratCom and the Supervisory Board. The questionnaire covers areas such as 
political contributions, memberships, lobbying activities and associated costs, both direct 
and indirect, as well as board positions held in external organizations. 
Members of the Supervisory Board are also asked to disclose any former public positions. 
The outcomes of this review provide assurance that Vopak’s leaders do not engage in 
direct lobbying or activities that conflict with the company’s Code of Conduct, 
sustainability policy, purpose, or strategic direction.
Vopak's Stakeholder Engagement Policy provides the framework for consistent, 
transparent, and structured interactions with stakeholders. The policy requires leaders to 
engage actively with local communities, mandates annual reviews of industry association 
memberships to ensure alignment with Vopak’s values and strategy, and prohibits political 
or religious donations made on behalf of the company. In addition, the policy promotes the 
implementation of Vopak WeConnect projects within each Business Unit to support and 
contribute to local communities.

Supervisory Board report
The Supervisory Board oversees and advises the Executive Board in performing its management tasks and guides the company’s operational 
and financial development. In performing their duties, the members of the Supervisory Board are guided by the interests of Vopak and all its 
stakeholders.
During 2025, the Supervisory Board held six regular meetings as well as one extra meeting. 
All regular meetings were held jointly with the Executive Board present. The plenary 
sessions of the Supervisory Board were accompanied by executive sessions, often with 
only the members of the Supervisory Board attending. Between meetings, the Chair of the 
Supervisory Board had regular contact with the CEO to discuss the current state of affairs 
of the company and to prepare for meetings, as was the case for the Chair of the 
Remuneration Committee, and the Chair of the Audit Committee with the CFO. In 2025, the 
average attendance at the regular and additional meetings combined was 95.2%.
Key developments
Strategy is one of the Supervisory Board’s main priorities and is an integral part of its 
considerations and decision making processes. This includes evaluating the way the 
Executive Board implements Vopak’s strategy for long-term value creation and promotes a 
culture aimed at creating value. The Improve, Grow, Accelerate strategy, which was 
developed with active involvement of the Supervisory Board, strengthens the foundation 
of the company and drives progress in the energy transition, growing the base in ITL and 
gas and optimizing the performance of the core portfolio. It also takes into account key 
global trends like the energy transition, aging assets, the regulatory landscape and ESG. 
Execution of the strategy, the progress made and the main risks associated, were regularly 
discussed this year with the Executive Board. The financial framework is aligned with the 
Improve, Grow, Accelerate strategy, emphasizing the ambition to become more cash 
focused and keeping a disciplined focus on capital allocation. This approach prioritizes a 
robust balance sheet, maintaining a healthy leverage ratio, returning value to shareholders 
through the progressive dividend policy and a share buyback program during 2025 and 
investing in attractive and accretive growth projects.
The Supervisory Board is involved in reviewing the execution of the company’s strategy by 
means of an in-depth dialogue. A three day strategy session was held in the Netherlands, 
which was combined with a visit to the Gate terminal in Rotterdam. New business 
opportunities are always assessed against their strategic rationale and the principal risks 
for both the short and long-term are evaluated thoroughly. 
Choices proposed by management can thereby be challenged and the underlying 
arguments weighed against each other. The Improve component of the strategy focuses 
on improving the financial and sustainability performance across the portfolio, and the 
Accelerate component aims for a portfolio transition across the world towards low-carbon 
fuels, ammonia, and CO  infrastructure by re-using existing assets and exploring 
greenfield opportunities. Overall the company appears well-positioned to leverage the 
market fundamentals and energy transition opportunities. At the same time the company 
remains sensitive to changes in the global operating landscape including geopolitical and 
macroeconomic uncertainty as well as slowing momentum in some aspects of the energy 
transition.
Important topics discussed by the Supervisory Board in 2025 include sustainability, 
digitalisation and sustaining capex programs. Sustainability is an important driver for the 
strategy and is a standard item on the agenda of the Supervisory Board. The approach 
towards sustainability is ambitious and performance driven with a balanced roadmap 
focusing on care for people, planet and profit. The aim is to reduce the company’s own 
environmental and carbon footprint by decarbonizing existing and future operations. In this 
way, the company remains a responsible member of society, being mindful of the potential 
impact of the business activities on people’s safety and health and the environment. Safety 
is a top priority ESG topic and is given ample time in the Supervisory Board meetings. This 
is also the case for diversity and human rights. Vopak is a multicultural company that 
continues to strive for a diverse workforce including people from different cultures, 
nationalities and beliefs. The standards on human rights and decent work are laid down in 
Vopak’s Code of Conduct and the Vopak Human Rights Policy. The company aspires to 
play an active role in the energy and feedstock transition and become net-zero by 2050 by 
constantly reducing its environmental footprint and greenhouse gas emissions. This 
ambition is laid down in a comprehensive roadmap with a CO  reduction target for scope 1 
and 2 of 30% by 2030 versus 2021, which requires a 45-60% reduction of CO  emissions 
from the current asset base as the company also needs to accommodate growth.

The Supervisory Board recognizes its own role in the company’s corporate governance 
structure, with members receiving updates and information to adequately fulfill their roles 
and responsibilities. Ongoing education is an important part of good governance. As part of 
the induction program, new members of the Supervisory Board visit various terminal 
locations and meet with business units and local management. They also attend induction 
sessions at which they are informed about financial, reporting, internal audit, HR, 
commercial and business development, IT, legal and governance related affairs.
All Supervisory Board members, except for one, as permitted by the Dutch Corporate 
Governance Code, qualify as independent in the meaning of best practice provision 2.1.7. 
Mr. De Visser does not satisfy all independence criteria. If a member of the Supervisory 
Board has a direct or indirect personal conflict of interest with Vopak, such member will 
not participate in the deliberations and the decision making of the Supervisory Board on 
the matter concerned.
The Supervisory Board has three committees: the Audit Committee, the Nomination 
Committee and the Remuneration Committee. Their roles are described below in more 
detail. The committees generate, review and discuss detailed information and prepare 
recommendations relating to their specific areas, while the full Supervisory Board retains 
overall responsibility and always takes the final decisions. In each case, the Committee 
Chair reports the Committee’s main considerations and findings to the full Supervisory 
Board, usually immediately after the relevant Committee meeting.
The Audit Committee assists the Supervisory Board in its responsibility to oversee Vopak’s 
financing, financial statements, financial and sustainability reporting, compliance and 
system of internal business controls, risk management and audit findings. Non-financial 
topics are also reviewed as part of risk management including cybersecurity and Fraud and 
Speak-Up reportings. The Remuneration Committee primarily makes recommendations 
regarding the remuneration policy and remuneration packages of the Executive Board and 
the Supervisory Board.
The composition of the Supervisory Board is such that relevant business know-how and 
adequate understanding of ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) related issues is 
directly available and embedded in the board governance structure. Also because of the 
importance of the ESG related issues, it was decided not to institute a separate ESG 
Committee and embed this directly with the Supervisory Board. The Supervisory Board is 
directly involved in matters where these relate to and/or concern the various areas of ESG 
including the development and integration of ESG in the company and its strategy, ESG 
priority setting and ESG related KPIs and connected target setting, compliance with 
applicable laws and regulations in the field of ESG. 
The Supervisory Board will generally monitor relevant ESG developments to enable it to 
advise and challenge the Executive Board with respect to ESG related matters on a regular 
basis and take any other action in the context of ESG.

reflect the Vopak culture, being clear and transparent. We developed the policies to foster

The Executive Board Remuneration Policy is designed to foster long-term success and 
sustainable value creation at Vopak. We ensure this by directly linking the Executive 
Board's short-term and long-term variable compensation to the successful execution and 
realization of Vopak’s strategy. This approach drives strong alignment with the interests of 
our shareholders, employees, and other stakeholders over both the short and long term.

Financial KPIs
Proportional EBITDA
Proportional EBITDA is the first of the two main - and most appropriate- short-term drivers 
to generate the cash flow required to realize Vopak's strategic ambitions and to deliver the 
expected returns to shareholders.
The performance indicator is used to evaluate Vopak's core corporate profitability and 
operating performance.
EBITDA is defined as net income before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization. 
Proportional operating capex
Proportional operating capex is the second of the two main and most appropriate short- 
term drivers to generate the cash flow required to realize Vopak's strategic ambitions and 
to deliver the expected returns to shareholders.
This performance indicator is used by the company to maintain and improve its service 
delivery and performance  in future years. 
Operating capex is defined as the annual capital expenditures spent on projects and 
activities required to acquire, upgrade and maintain the physical asset base of the 
company ("sustaining capex"), the tangible and intangible IT asset base of the company 
("IT capex") and any other intangible asset base of the company ("service capex"). 
Non-financial KPIs
To measure the frontline execution, targets are set for safety and customer service.
Safety
Vopak’s "License to Operate" and its "License to Grow" are conditional upon our ability to 
operate with care for safety, health and the environment. Vopak's ambition is to be the 
sustainability leader in the industry and to be as good as the safest and most sustainable 
of our customers.
Process safety and the occupational health and safety of employees and contractors are 
the company’s top priorities. The long-term aim is zero incidents and no serious harm to 
anybody working at a Vopak facility.
Safety is measured by means of two equally weighted quantitative performance criteria:
Customer service
Vopak focuses on driving service performance to the next level to achieve its commercial 
and customer satisfaction goals. The realization of our customer service goals is directed 
by ambitious, quantitative Net Promoter Scores. The payout of the actual incentive is 
conditional on a participation rate of ≥ 30%.
Specific Executive Board targets
Each year, targets for the Executive Board are selected from the areas in the company’s 
strategy that are typically not or insufficiently addressed by other KPIs in the Executive 
Board STIP and LTSP programs. The performance indicators selected measure the 
progress of Vopak’s sustainability ambition.
Process safety event rate (PSER); PSER is measured as the total number of Tier 1 & 2 
process incidents on Vopak sites, including joint ventures, per 200,000 available working 
hours (own staff + contractors).
•
Total injury rate (TIR); TIR is measured as the total number of all reportable injuries per 
200,000 available working hours (own staff and contractors). In the event of an 
employee or contractor fatality, the payout on TIR will be reduced by 50%. In case of two 
or more fatalities during the performance year, the payout on TIR will be adjusted 
downward to zero.

Proportional operating cash return (OCR)
This performance indicator reflects improvements in the performance of the portfolio. It 
reflects Vopak's longer-term sustainable cash flow generation and long-term sustainable 
returns delivery to shareholders. It is the metric of Vopak’s long-term sustainable cash flow 
generation as a portion of invested capital. 
OCR (%) is defined as operating free cash flow divided by capital employed, excluding 
exceptional items.
It is measured as the average of end values at December 31 of years 1, 2 and 3 in the 
applicable performance year.
To establish a like-for-like comparison with the preset targets, the actual realization of the 
result is corrected for acquisitions, divestments, and material impairments that take place 
after target-setting, as well as for the impact of investment proposals approved by the 
Executive Board after target-setting. It is not corrected for foreign currency translation 
effects.
Proportional capex committed to industrial, gas & other terminals
This indicator measures the strategic portfolio shift toward industrial, gas and other 
terminals. As defined in Shaping the Future, the ambition is to invest EUR 2.6 billion in 
industrial, gas and other terminals by 2030.
Capex committed to industrial, gas and other terminals is defined as the share of 
committed investments in qualifying industrial, gas and other terminals investments, within 
the framework and targets of return established by the Supervisory Board. Among others, 
the following investments qualify: the acquisition of industrial, gas and other terminals 
(based on Vopak’s share in the enterprise value of the company and all potential - 
proportional - earn outs); projects in existing terminals and greenfield project 
developments that are classified as industrial, gas and other such as: capacity expansions 
and associated infrastructure investments.

LTSP (conditional) award and vesting
LTSP (conditional) award and grant
Each year, a conditional award of performance shares, known as the "grant", is  made to 
the individual Executive Board members. This grant is calculated based on the member's 
annual base salary, the applicable target incentive opportunity, and the prevailing share 
price, which is the average share price (Close of Business) from the preceding quartile. 
Proration applies if a new member is promoted internally after May 1 or hired externally 
after January 1.
LTSP vesting and performance evaluation
The vesting of each grant is scheduled to occur immediately after the first Annual General 
Meeting following the end of the three-year performance period. Vesting is always subject 
to the preset performance and other conditions being met.
At the conclusion of the three-year performance period, we evaluate performance against 
the targets. The number of shares that vest and are delivered to individual Executive Board 
members reflects the performance achieved against these preset targets.
As long as awards under the LTSP remain unvested, Executive Board members are only 
eligible for vesting; no entitlement is established. Vesting requires meeting at least the 
minimum performance and other conditions.
The Supervisory Board has the discretionary powers to make the decision to vest an 
award or to lapse an award at any time between the date of award and the vesting date, 
including after Executive Board members have left the company. Accelerated vesting or a 
guaranteed vesting outcome does not apply, unless extraordinary circumstances occur 
(such as the death of a – formerly - eligible Executive Board member).
The Supervisory Board has the discretionary authority to adjust the number of LTSP shares 
delivered, if it is of the opinion that such adjustment(s) would produce a fairer reflection of 
the performance of Vopak and/ or of the individual members of the Executive Board. Such 
adjustment(s) are made within the limits of the policy, i.e. the total number of vesting LTSP 
shares so decided upon will remain within the original 0% to 150% pay-out/ vesting range.
In the event that an individual Executive Board member is considered to have left the 
company on grounds within his/ her control, the Supervisory Board will decide on a 
discretionary basis how any outstanding unvested awards made to this Executive Board 
member earlier will be affected.
In the case of an Executive Board member leaving the company in good standing - at the 
discretion of the Supervisory Board- but in any case including (force majeure) situations 
such as death, longer-term disability, no reappointment after the end of the four-year 
service period or a restructuring of the Board, any awards made under the company's 
Executive Board LTSP programs that have not yet vested on the date of termination will be 
prorated on the basis of the months served of the full performance period of 36 months.

is equal to the target number of shares awarded (in case of the unvested shares thus

announcement of such event, and/ or (b) another share-based instrument now available as 
a result of such event; and, furthermore, it may (iv) take whatever other steps are 
considered appropriate  to arrive at a fair compensation outcome as intended under the 
company’s Executive Board LTSP programs.
Share ownership
Executive Board members are required to own, at all times, a minimum number of company 
shares acquired under the company’s LTIP while serving as Executive Board member.
Only company shares vested to them under the company’s LTIPs and in excess of this 
minimum may be transferred or sold by the member of the Executive Board. Such a 
transfer or sale is subject to the company’s insider trading policy and other legal 
requirements. New Executive Board members accrue their required shareholding over time 
via the vesting of the LTSP awards. Company shares acquired via private investments are 
not subject to this minimum portfolio requirement, and therefore do not count toward this 
threshold either.
Under the Dutch Corporate Governance Code, Executive Board members are required to 
hold shares acquired under company long-term share compensation plans for a minimum 
of five years after the date on which these shares were (conditionally) awarded. The 
Supervisory Board believes that the requirement  to hold a minimum portfolio of shares 
continuously throughout one's tenure on the Board is better suited to the longer-term 
nature of Vopak’s strategy and line of business. On a day-to-day continuous basis, Vopak’s 
shareholding requirement for Executive Board members results in a total number of shares 
vested and delivered to individual Executive Board members, and subsequently restricted 
from further sale, that is similar or higher compared to the shareholding requirement 
included in the Dutch Corporate Governance Code, such depending on the number of 
shares awarded that actually vest.
Pension
Vopak’s Executive Board members participate in the same company pension plan as other 
staff employed by Vopak in the Netherlands. As of January 1, 2018, this is a defined 
contribution plan funded by contributions from both the company and participating 
employees. The retirement age under the Vopak pension plan is set at age 68 and includes 
various early retirement options on a cost neutral basis. In the calculation of the 
pensionable base salary, an offset for state pension entitlements, and a part of the actual 
annual bonus paid out in the year at hand under the STIP to a maximum of 15% of the 
pensionable base salary, are included. Regarding to death and disability, risk insurances 
apply. The pension plan includes three contribution arrangements, dependent on annual 
pensionable salary levels:
For the CEO, this minimum shareholding requirement is the number of shares with a 
value equivalent to two (2) times the annual base salary.
•
For the CFO this minimum shareholding requirement is the number of shares with a value 
equivalent to one (1) time annual base salary.
•
Basic arrangement for that part of the annual pensionable salary up to EUR 75,486 
(2025)
•
Surplus arrangement for that part of the annual pensionable salary from EUR 75,486 up 
to EUR 137,800 (2025)
•
Net Surplus arrangement for that part of the annual pensionable salary above EUR 
137,800 (2025). Due to Dutch fiscal regulations, the employer contributions to this 
arrangement are made to participants in the form of gross cash compensation subject to 
tax withholdings, which can be used to fund a voluntary net defined contribution plan.

The caps in these three arrangements are set by the Board of the Vopak Pension Fund and

Any changes in these caps are not subject to the further approval of the Annual General

For Executive Board members who were employed by or in the service of the company 
prior to January 1,  2015, no employee contributions are required, also not in the case their 
Executive Board membership began after January 1, 2015 as a result of an internal 
promotion. For Executive Board members joining the company as a new employee or as an 
Executive Board member, an employee contribution of 4% of their gross salary is withheld, 
in line with the 4% employee contribution obligations for all Vopak employees in the 
Netherlands.
In line with the arrangements in place for all Vopak employees in the Netherlands, 
Executive Board members are eligible for a gross cash allowance of 1.5% of their annual 
base salary (subject to tax withholdings). This is the so-called well-being allowance.
Benefits and other emoluments
Additionally, benefits and other emoluments are provided for in line with the Vopak 
Netherlands policies, plans and arrangements which apply to all Vopak staff in the 
Netherlands.
The company will provide the necessary business means to Executive Board members as 
required for the execution of their role and responsibilities. Their use is for business 
purposes only and is subject to the general policies that apply to all staff which among 
things restricts the use of these means for private purposes where applicable.
Reasonable expenses will only be reimbursed to individual Executive Board members, if 
these are incurred while performing their duties. The approval of such business expenses 
follows the Vopak policies and procedures for such expenses.
For Executive Board members who are recruited externally, the Supervisory Board may 
decide to provide additional one-off remuneration in the form of a sign-on bonus and/ or a 
buy-out arrangement (to compensate for any variable compensation forfeited as a result of 
joining Vopak), if this would be deemed fair and appropriate and in line with established 
market practices. 
In addition, should Executive Board members come from abroad, they may be eligible for 
expatriate benefits in cash or in kind, including tax assistance, in line with the Vopak global 
mobility policies applicable to Vopak staff, depending on personal circumstances.
The company will not provide any personal loan, advance or guarantee to Executive Board 
members.
Appointment and termination of Executive Board members
Executive Board members are (re-)appointed for a term of four years in accordance with 
legal and regulatory requirements. Executive Board appointments are governed by Dutch 
employment law and aligned with the current Dutch Corporate Governance Code. Vopak 
Executive Board agreements include confidentiality, non-compete and non-solicitation 
clauses.
For Executive Board members, any additional remuneration (“sign-on”) paid upon 
recruitment, compensation for a (non-voluntary) (early) termination of appointment 
(“severance pay”), or a change-in-control is decided by the Supervisory Board, taking into 
account standards of reasonableness and fairness and the Dutch Corporate Governance 
Code. In any case, a severance payment will not exceed one year’s fixed remuneration. No 
severance will be paid in the event of voluntary resignation by, or seriously culpable or 
negligent behavior on the part of, the individual Executive Board member.
Supervisory Board Remuneration
The Supervisory Board remuneration policy is designed to support the Supervisory Board 
in duly and independently executing its duties and contributing to the realization of 
Vopak’s strategic objectives. This includes fostering longer-term value creation for the 
company and its stakeholders.
The policy achieves this by providing compensation that consists of fixed elements only, 
ensuring alignment with the interests of our stakeholders and society at large. 
Remuneration levels are set to be sustainable and competitive within the context of the 
Netherlands.

To create a fair and representative reference point, we include our entire global base of

Governance
Proposals for the Supervisory Board Policy or Executive Board Remuneration policy, 
including remuneration packages provided to individual Board members, are determined 
by the Supervisory Board, based on recommendations of the Remuneration Committee 
supported by internal and external independent specialists, before being submitted to the 
AGM for approval. Decisions regarding the Executive Board Remuneration Policy and the 
remuneration of individual Executive Board members are made in the Executive Board's 
absence. However, the Remuneration Committee acknowledges the views of individual 
Executive Board members regarding the policy and their own individual compensation. Any 
material alterations and/-or revisions to the Supervisory Board policy or Executive Board 
Remuneration policy are submitted to the AGM for approval. If either policy remains 
unaltered within four years of the most recent AGM approval, it will be put forward to the 
AGM for confirmation of approval. Changes in the Vopak Netherlands benefits and 
emoluments policies, plans, and/-or arrangements applicable to all Vopak non-CLA staff, 
and for which Executive Board members are also eligible, follow the regular legal and 
company governance processes for such changes. In the event that changes on any of 
these policies, plans and/ or arrangements affect the entitlements of Executive Board 
members under these policies, such changes are not subject to the AGM's approval. For 
further information on governance, please refer to the section Corporate Governance in 
this Annual Report.
Temporary derogation from the policy
As determined by the Dutch Civil Code, derogation from these Supervisory Board and 
Executive Board remuneration policies is only allowed under exceptional circumstances 
and for a limited time under the following conditions:
If between AGMs, there are changes in applicable legislation and/-or regulation that result 
in a conflict with the Supervisory Board and Executive Board remuneration policies, or part 
thereof, the Supervisory Board may deviate from these policies with immediate effect to 
ensure compliance. Such a deviation does not constitute a temporary derogation of the 
policy. The Supervisory Board will disclose the deviation in the subsequent remuneration 
report and submit a proposal to the shareholders at the subsequent AGM that complies 
with the new legislation and/-or regulations.
The Supervisory Board (pre-)approves the derogation on the basis of an assessment of 
the rationale, the provision being derogated, the duration of the derogation, the impact 
on individual Supervisory Board and/-or Executive Board members, and the extent to 
which the derogation complies with the applicable rules and regulations. The derogation, 
its details, and the outcome of the assessment are disclosed in the remuneration report 
of the annual report of the year in which the temporary derogation took place.
•
If the derogation results in a material change to the Supervisory Board fees and- or 
Executive Board remuneration structures or levels, or in any other material condition of 
these policies, it will be presented to the subsequent AGM for approval, irrespective of 
whether the derogation results in a revision of these policies or not.
•
The derogation may be applicable to any provision in these policies, as long as it (i) 
aligns with the general remuneration objectives and principles as described in these 
policies; (ii) is  required in order to serve the long-term interests and sustainability of

Corporate Governance
Vopak is incorporated and based in the Netherlands. As a result, Vopak’s governance structure is based on the requirements of Dutch legislation 
including securities laws, the company’s articles of association, complemented by internal policies and procedures. Given the worldwide 
exposure of its businesses, the international context is of vital importance and relevant international developments are closely monitored.
Good corporate governance is a key component of Vopak’s way of doing business and is 
embedded in its core values. The corporate governance is supported by a strong focus on 
integrity, transparency and clear and timely communication. Good governance and proper 
supervision are important prerequisites for generating and maintaining trust in the 
company.
Vopak’s business, financial and investor strategy is focused on long-term value creation for 
the company and its affiliated enterprises as formulated by the Executive Board under the 
guidance of the Supervisory Board. Value creation is closely connected with the culture 
within the company, the view on sustainability matters and long-term value creation 
requires a culture aimed at that. Long-term value creation also requires awareness and 
anticipation of new developments in technology that can contribute to the continuing 
success of the company. All stakeholder interests are hereby taken into careful 
consideration.
The leadership style within Vopak stimulates a culture that promotes desired behavior and 
encourages employees to act with integrity and to lead by example. By communicating this 
culture with its corresponding values, incorporating it into the enterprise and maintaining it, 
guidance is provided in making everyday decisions and monitoring ethical conduct by 
people in all tiers of the organization.
The top of the company has regular contact with employees at all levels of the company as 
it is essential to know how the culture is experienced within the organization. Culture is 
also monitored via the employee engagement survey. More information on the culture 
within Vopak is provided in the People Leadership chapter.
The Vopak Code of Conduct is based on the Vopak corporate values to provide the 
conditions for a healthy culture and effectively encourage an atmosphere of openness. 
Neither leadership nor culture are considered tick the box items or treated as such. 
All Vopak employees, partners, contractors and suppliers are required to adhere explicitly 
to the Code of Conduct. Compliance is regularly checked for example as part of the CSRA 
and internal business audits. These monitoring tools also show and measure the 
effectiveness of the Code of Conduct. Vopak complies with the principles and best 
practices laid down in the 2025 Dutch Corporate Governance Code (the Code). The only 
two exceptions are explained in this annual report.
Set-up and policy
Vopak aims to strike a sound balance between the interests of the company’s various 
stakeholders. Integrity, openness, supervision, transparent reporting and accountability are 
the cornerstones of the corporate governance policy. The company has also developed a 
clear policy with regard to reporting for financial matters and sustainability. Vopak confirms 
that the principles reflected in the Code are applied by Vopak except for the deviations 
from the Code that are explained in the following paragraphs.
Vopak has a two-tier governance structure requiring a well-managed relationship between 
the Executive Board solely composed of executive directors and the Supervisory Board 
solely composed of non-executive directors. The two Boards are independent of each 
other and have their own roles and responsibilities in the governance structure.
The Executive Board is responsible for the management of the company and for the 
realization of its objectives. These include the objectives for strategy and policy, health, 
safety, the environment (part of sustainability), quality, as well as results.
The Executive Board is assisted in fulfilling its responsibilities by the Risk Committee, the 
Compliance Committee and the Disclosure Committee. The activities of the Risk 
Committee include facilitating and challenging risk reporting within the company, providing 
oversight of main risks and related risk management activities.
