Risk management
The credit risk with regard to trade receivables and lease receivables from customers is 
limited as the value of the product stored for these clients usually exceeds the value of the 
receivables and Vopak generally has the right of retention although other claims may have 
priority ranking over the right of retention in a bankruptcy case. Vopak constantly monitors 
the outstanding receivables and the value of the stored products. See note 4.2 for further 
details.
Vopak has spread its cash and cash equivalents and other liquidity investments across a 
select group of high rated financial institutions while daily limiting the cash and cash 
equivalents within the Group and assessing the exposure to each financial institution. 
Vopak applies credit limits per institution, depending on their credit ratings and credit 
default swap spread, and regularly reviews these limits. 
These treasury activities are concluded with financial institutions that have at least an A- 
 Standard & Poor's credit rating or equivalent rating. At 31 December 2025, the maximum 
risk in the event of the default of a single financial institution amounted to 
EUR 32.0 million (2024: EUR 41.6 million).
The derivative financial instruments will be settled on a gross basis. The credit risk of 
derivative financial instruments with a positive value is mitigated by ISDA Master 
Agreements with counterparties, which have the option to settle all gross amounts on a 
net basis in the event of a default of the counterparty, and by setting qualitative and 
financial limits for the derivative counterparties. The Group maintains a control system that 
includes the authorization, reporting and monitoring of derivative activities including the 
Credit Default Swaps developments of counterparties observed on the secondary market. 
Vopak believes there are no material credit risks related to derivatives in the Group's 
financial position. At year-end 2025, the derivatives with a counterparty credit risk 
amounted to nil (2024: EUR 7.4 million).
Assessing the financial positions of customers and other counterparties is part of the 
Group's credit risk management and tendering process; however, this cannot exclude all 
credit risk.
Note 6.7 Liquidity risk
The primary objective of liquidity management is providing sufficient cash and cash 
equivalents at all times to enable Vopak to meet its payment obligations.
Cash management
The liquidity requirements are monitored continuously and funding is planned in such a 
way as to avoid excessive short-term financing needs. The long-term liquidity risk is 
assessed prior to every major investment obligation. Active cash management is a daily 
responsibility and the liquidity requirements are identified each quarter based on thorough 
scenario planning. Surplus cash is invested, if available, in interest-bearing accounts and 
deposit accounts.
Vopak's Global Treasury function acts as an in-house bank that allocates funds internally, 
which are raised centrally within the Group. Surplus cash held by the operating entities 
over and above balances required for working capital management is transferred to Global 
Treasury and operating companies are normally funded by a combination of equity and 
inter-company loans. 
Exceptions to this are the bank loan of EUR 149.1 million (SGD 225.0 million of which SGD 
200.0 million term loan and SGD 25.0 million revolving credit facility), drawdowns under 
the revolving credit facilities of Vopak Terminals Singapore Pte. Ltd., which have been 
raised locally. Both instruments are sustainability linked.
Joint ventures and associates, where possible, are normally funded optimally with external 
debt on a non-recourse basis for Vopak, taking into account local circumstances and 
contractual obligations. Reference is made to note 9.8 for more information with regard to 
commitments and guarantees provided to joint ventures and associates.

Material accounting policies
Share-based compensation
The fair value of equity-settled share-based compensation plans is determined at the date 
of granting and expensed in the statement of income based on the Group's estimate of the 
shares that will eventually vest over the period in which the service is rendered (vesting 
period) with a corresponding adjustment directly in equity. The fair value of cash-settled 
share-based compensation plans is determined at the date of granting and is remeasured 
at each reporting date until the liability is settled and is recognized over the vesting period 
as an expense to the extent to which participants have rendered services to date.
Generally, the compensation cost is recognized on a straight-line basis over the vesting 
period. At the end of each period, the Company revises its estimates of the number of 
shares that are expected to vest based on the non-market vesting and service conditions. 
It recognizes the impact of the revision to original estimates, if any, in profit or loss, with a 
corresponding adjustment to equity. Where shares are forfeited due to a failure by the 
employee to satisfy the service conditions, any expenses previously recognized in relation 
to such shares are reversed effective from the date of the forfeiture. For a detailed 
description of the LTSP reference is made to the remuneration report.

Note 8.1 Income taxes
Material accounting policies
Income tax expense comprises current and deferred tax. Tax is recognized in profit or loss, 
except to the extent that it relates to a business combination, or to items recognized 
directly in equity or in other comprehensive income.
Current taxes are the expected taxes payable to or recoverable from taxation authorities 
regarding the taxable profit or loss for the year, using tax rates substantively enacted at 
the end of the reporting period, including adjustments to tax positions of prior years.
Deferred taxes are recognized using the liability method on all taxable temporary 
differences between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities for financial reporting 
purposes and their respective tax bases. Deferred tax liabilities are recognized for all 
taxable temporary differences, except for those arising from: the initial recognition of 
goodwill; the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction which is not a 
business combination and, at the time of the transaction, affects neither accounting profit 
nor taxable profit and does not give rise to equal taxable and deductible temporary 
differences; and differences relating to investments in subsidiaries to the extent that the 
Group is able to control the timing of the reversal and it is probable that they will not 
reverse in the foreseeable future. 
Deferred tax assets, including those arising from unused tax losses and credits, are 
recognized to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available 
against which these can be utilized. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the 
tax rates that are expected to apply to the period when the asset is realized or the liability 
is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively 
enacted by the end of the reporting period. They are stated at nominal value.  
The Group recognizes liabilities for uncertain tax treatments based on estimates of 
whether additional taxes will be due. Where the final tax outcome differs from the amounts 
initially recorded, such differences will impact the current and deferred income tax assets 
and liabilities in the period in which such determination is made.  
Withholding taxes and other taxes on the distribution of retained earnings of subsidiaries 
are recognized as a deferred tax liability, except to the extent that the Group is able to 
control the timing of the distribution and it is probable that the distribution will not occur in 
the foreseeable future.

OECD Pillar Two model rules
The Group is within the scope of the OECD Pillar Two model rules as Vopak both exceeds 
the annual revenue threshold of EUR 750 million and is included in the consolidation 
scope of HAL. Pillar Two legislation entered into force on 31 December 2023 in the 
Netherlands, the jurisdiction in which Vopak is incorporated, and is effective for the 
Group's financial year beginning 1 January 2024. The Group applies the exception to 
recognizing and disclosing information about deferred tax assets and liabilities related to 
Pillar Two income taxes, as provided in the amendments to IAS 12 issued in May 2023. As 
a result, the Group neither recognizes nor discloses information about deferred tax assets 
and liabilities related to Pillar Two income taxes.
The Group is in scope of the enacted or substantively enacted legislation and has 
performed an assessment of the Group's potential exposure to Pillar Two income taxes. 
Under the legislation, the Group is liable to pay a top-up tax for the difference between its 
GloBE effective tax rate per jurisdiction and the 15% minimum rate. The assessment of the 
potential exposure to Pillar Two income taxes is based on the most recent tax filings, 
country-by-country reporting and financial statements of the constituent entities in the 
Group. Based on the assessment and application of the transitional safe harbour relief, the 
Group does not expect to have an exposure for Pillar Two income taxes for any of its 
constituent entities included in the consolidation scope. For several jurisdictions, the 
Group performed a detailed Pillar Two GloBE calculation based upon which it concluded 
that there is no top-up tax liability for the financial year 2025 (2024: nil). Furthermore, the 
OECD Pillar Model rules are also applicable to joint ventures which are not included in the 
Group's consolidation scope, but in which the Group holds a(n) (in)direct ownership 
percentage of at least 50%. For these equity-accounted joint ventures an assessment of 
the potential exposure to Pillar Two income taxes has also been made. Based on this 
assessment the current tax expense related to Pillar Two income taxes for the financial 
year 2025 amounts to EUR 0.6 million (2024: EUR 0.6 million).

Note 9.3 Macro-economic and geopolitical uncertainty
Vopak operates in 21 countries that have different degrees of political, legal and fiscal 
stability. This exposes Vopak to a wide range of political- and country risks that could 
result in changes to laws and regulations.
Vopak plays a critical role in delivering energy security for global supply chains. In 2025, 
this role was important, as geopolitical tensions continued to rise in many regions. The 
Russia-Ukraine war and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, in particular, and the 
associated sanctions continued to affect the availability, flows, and pricing of energy 
products. China’s technological advancements and ongoing trade tensions with the US 
have given rise to geopolitical tensions.
Vopak is monitoring the geopolitical situations and volatility in trade dynamics (including 
tariffs) closely and is fully committed to adhere to relevant sanctions, laws and regulations. 
As governments try to ensure energy security and affordability, Vopak adheres to 
applicable government regulations with regards to energy imports from Russia.
The Russia-Ukraine war and the international sanction regimes make the market situation 
volatile and uncertain. Direct impact is assessed to be mainly in Vopak’s Europoort terminal 
and to be limited on Vopak’s group level. There is, however, an indirect exposure through 
factors such as utility prices, inflation, market conditions and exchange rates, which was 
considered during the individual asset valuation performed during 2025. Vopak continues 
to closely monitor the developments and takes measures to adapt to the changed factors.
Vopak’s strategy is robust and unchanged. An effective control and governance structure 
to respond to the impact of the global pandemic, with continued decision-making to 
support business execution and well-being of people, has been put in place. Operational 
and financial performance, cash flows and our financial position have not been significantly 
affected. Our financial results reflect our resilient business performance.
Note 9.4 Pensions and other employee benefits
The majority of employees are either covered by defined benefit plans, defined 
contribution plans or mandatory external pension plans. The defined benefit plans are 
plans that apply in the following countries: the United States, Germany and Belgium. These 
countries mostly operate final-pay pension plans, administrated by pension funds separate 
from the company.
Material accounting policies
Defined benefit plans
The Group's net pension obligation is calculated by an independent actuary, using the 
projected unit credit method. This calculation is performed separately for each plan by 
estimating the amount of the benefit that employees have earned in relation to their past 
services. The liability recognized in the balance sheet is the present value of these 
benefits at the end of the reporting period (defined benefit obligation) less the fair value of 
plan assets. The defined benefit obligation is determined by discounting the estimated 
future cash flows using interest rates of high-quality corporate bonds with durations 
matching the expected terms of the benefits.
The increase in the defined benefit obligation due to the passage of time and the expected 
return on plan assets, using the same interest rate as for the defined benefit obligation, are 
included in the pension costs.
Past-service costs are recognized immediately in the statement of income. 
Remeasurements, comprising of the effect of the asset ceiling and actuarial gains and 
losses arising from experience adjustments and changes in actuarial assumptions are 
recognized in equity via Other comprehensive income in the period in which they 
arise. Remeasurements are not reclassified to profit or loss in subsequent periods.
When a plan is changed, settled or when a plan is curtailed, the resulting change in the 
defined benefit obligation that relates to past-service or the gain or loss on curtailment is 
recognized immediately in the statement of income under Personnel expenses. The Group 
recognizes gains and losses on the settlement of a defined benefit plan when the 
settlement occurs.
Defined contribution plans
Contributions to defined contribution plans are recognized as an expense in the statement 
of income as incurred.

Note 9.5 Provisions
Material accounting policies
Provisions are recognized for legal or constructive obligations that arose from past events, 
the amount of which, though uncertain, can be reliably estimated and where it is probable 
that the settlement of the obligations will entail a cash outflow. Provisions are measured at 
the present value of the expenditures expected to be required to settle the obligation 
using a pre-tax rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money 
and the risks specific to the obligation. The increase in the provision due to the passage of 
time is recognized as interest expense.
In accordance with current legislation, environmental plans and other measures to be 
adopted are agreed with local, regional and national authorities as appropriate. As soon as 
such plans are approved or other statutory obligations arise, a provision is formed based 
on the most reliable estimate possible of the future expenses.
A provision for reorganization is recognized when Vopak has approved a detailed and 
formalized reorganization plan and when the reorganization has either commenced or 
been announced.
A number of sites have to be restored to their original condition before being handed back 
at the end of the contractual period. If and when it is probable that a site will be 
decommissioned a provision is formed based on the most reliable estimate possible of 
future expenses.
Provisions for other deferred long-term employee benefits, other than pensions and other 
employee benefits, for example, redundancy benefits, anniversary incentives and 
long-term remuneration settled in cash, are calculated using the method for defined 
benefit plans. Any actuarial results arising are recognized immediately in the statement of 
income. The same applies to any changes relating to past service.
 Key accounting estimates and judgments 
The amount recognized as a provision is management's best estimate of the amount required to 
settle the obligation. The outcome depends on future events that are uncertain by nature. In 
assessing the likely outcome of lawsuits and tax disputes, management also bases its assessment 
on external legal assistance and established precedents.
The Group is exposed to risks regarding environmental obligations arising from past activities. For 
example, a number of sites have to be decontaminated before being handed back at the end of 
the contractual period. Under current legislation, environmental plans and any other measures to 
be adopted have to be agreed with local, regional and national authorities as appropriate. As soon 
as such plans have been approved or other legal obligations arose, a provision is formed based on 
the most reliable estimate of possible future expenses. Given the degree of complexity and 
uncertainty in making such estimates, this does not guarantee that no additional costs will arise in 
the future. 
 
Termination benefits are payable when employment is terminated by the Group before the normal 
retirement date, or when an employee accepts voluntary redundancy in exchange for these 
benefits. The Group recognizes termination benefits at the earlier of the following dates: (a) when 
the group can no longer withdraw the offer of those benefits; and (b) when the entity recognizes 
costs for a restructuring that is within the scope of IAS 37 and involves the payment of 
terminations benefits.
In the case of an offer made to encourage voluntary redundancy, the termination benefits are 
measured based on the number of employees expected to accept the offer. Benefits falling due 
more than 12 months after the end of the reporting period are discounted to present value.

Material accounting policies
The group makes an irrevocable election on an investment-by-investment basis at the 
time of initial recognition to measure these investments either as:
Investments and other financial assets are measured at fair value (level 3). At initial 
recognition, the Group measures a financial asset at its fair value. Transaction costs of 
financial assets measured at FVPL are expensed in profit or loss, while these are 
recognized in Other comprehensive income for financial assets measured at FVOCI.
The Group subsequently measures all equity investments at fair value. Where the group’s 
management has elected to present fair value gains and losses on equity investments in 
OCI, there is no subsequent reclassification of fair value gains and losses to profit or loss 
following the derecognition of the investment. Dividends from such investments continue 
to be recognized in profit or loss as dividend income as part of the Other operating 
income. Reference is also made to note 2.4.

Determination of fair value for financial instruments
A number of the Group’s accounting policies and disclosures require the determination of 
fair value for the financial instruments. A fair value measurement is an estimate of the price 
that would be received upon the sale of an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly 
transaction between market participants at the measurement date. Where available, fair 
value measurements are derived from quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for 
identical assets or liabilities (level 1). In the absence of such information, other observable 
inputs, either directly (i.e. as prices) or indirectly (i.e. derived from prices), are used to 
estimate fair values (level 2). No material financial instruments were measured at fair value 
using level 3 (inputs not based on observable market data). Inputs derived from external 
sources are corroborated or otherwise verified, as appropriate.
The fair values of the Private Placements, revolving credit facility and other long-term bank 
loans are measured by discounting the future cash flows using observable market interest 
information (level 2) as no similar instrument is available due to the specific profiles of the 
instruments. The calculations include credit spreads based on the most recent borrowing 
contracts.
The fair values of interest rate swaps, cross-currency interest rate swaps and forward 
foreign exchange contracts are determined by discounting the future cash flows using the 
applicable period-end observable yield curve, taking into account credit risk and the risk of 
non-performance.
In view of the short-term nature or the magnitude of the amounts, the Group considers 
that the fair value of loans granted, trade and other receivables, cash and cash 
equivalents, bank overdrafts, credit facilities, other long-term loans and trade creditors are 
not materially different from their carrying value.
The fair value of the Other equity investments (level 3) are based on discounted cash flow 
projections based on reliable estimates of future cash flows or recent transactions.
The initial measurement at the trade date of all financial instruments is the fair value. 
Except for derivatives, the initial measurement of financial instruments is adjusted for 
directly attributable transaction costs.

Overview and context
Koninklijke Vopak N.V. is an independent tank storage provider, specializing in the storage 
and handling of liquid chemicals, gases and oil products and contributing to infrastructure 
solutions for low-carbon and renewable energies. The Group is comprised of several 
components and therefore we considered our group audit scope and approach as set out 
in the section ‘The scope of our group audit’.
As part of designing our audit, we determined materiality and assessed the risks of 
material misstatement in the financial statements. In particular, we considered where 
management made important judgements, for example, in respect of significant accounting 
estimates that involved making assumptions and considering future events that are 
inherently uncertain. In these considerations, we paid attention to, amongst others, the 
assumptions underlying the physical and transition risk related to climate change.
In Section 1 ‘Basis of preparation’, note 1.1 of the consolidated financial statements, the 
Group describes the areas of judgement in applying accounting policies and the key 
sources of estimation uncertainty. Given the significant estimation uncertainty and the 
related higher inherent risks of material misstatement in the valuation of property, plant 
and equipment, joint ventures and associates, we considered this matter as a key audit 
matter as set out in the section ‘Key audit matter’ of this report.
Koninklijke Vopak N.V. assessed the possible effects of climate change and its plans to 
meet the net zero commitments on its financial position, refer to note 1.1 Basis of 
preparation in the Consolidated financial statements. We discussed Koninklijke Vopak 
N.V.’s assessment and governance thereof with management and evaluated the potential 
impact on the financial position including underlying assumptions and estimates, including 
among others useful life of fixed assets, impairment considerations and/or environmental 
provisions. Please also refer to the Key audit matter ‘Impairment assessment of property, 
plant and equipment, joint ventures and associates’, where the impact and the approach 
thereon is described.
Other areas of focus, that were not considered as key audit matters, were amongst other: 
the partial dilution of interest in Aegis Vopak Terminal Limited ("AVTL"), the share buy-back 
program, the US private placement, organizational integration and restructuring charges 
and onerous contract charges at Vopak Gas Terminal ("VGT") in Singapore.
We ensured that the audit teams at both group and component level included the 
appropriate skills and competences which are needed for the audit of a provider of 
infrastructure solutions for storage and handling of essential products in energy and 
manufacturing industries. We therefore included experts and specialists in the areas of 
amongst others IT, tax, actuarial expertise, and valuation in our team.
First-year audit consideration
After our appointment as the Company’s auditors, we developed and executed a 
comprehensive transition plan. As part of this transition plan, we carried out a process of 
understanding the strategy of the Group, its business, its internal control environment and 
IT systems. We examined where and how this affected the Group’s and the Company’s 
financial statements and internal control framework. Additionally, we read the prior year 
financial statements, and we reviewed the predecessor auditor’s files and discussed and 
evaluated the outcome of the audit procedures included therein.
We attended all Audit Committee meetings since our appointment in April 2024. Based on 
these procedures, amongst others, we obtained sufficient and appropriate audit evidence 
regarding the opening balances. Furthermore, we prepared our risk assessment, our audit 
strategy and our audit plan for the year 2025, which we discussed with management and 
the Audit Committee.

manipulate accounting records and prepare fraudulent financial statements by overriding

Management's short-term and long-term incentives are determined based on a 
combination of key performance indicators (KPIs), with a significant portion of those being 
financial KPIs. Furthermore, as Vopak is a listed company, management could experience 
pressure to meet investor expectations.
That is why, in all our audit, we pay attention to the risk of management override of 
controls in:
The appropriateness of journal entries and other adjustments made in the preparation of 
the financial statements;

Identified risks
The risk of fraudulent financial reporting due to overstating the revenue
As part of our risk assessment and based on a presumption that there are risks of fraud in 
revenue recognition, we evaluated which types of revenue give rise to risk of material 
misstatement due to fraud.
Management receives bonuses, of which the size partly depends on the financial results 
achieved. In this context, management has been given specific targets for growth in 
turnover and results. This could lead to pressure on management to overstate revenue by 
posting manual adjustments or entering fictitious turnover.
Consequently, we deem the risk of fraud in revenue recognition to be mainly prevalent in 
the area of fictitious revenue transactions driven by journal entries and other adjustments 
made in the financial closing process and preparation of the financial statements.
We defined accuracy and existence/occurrence assertions as those having significant risk 
for all revenue streams.

We evaluated the design and implementation of the internal control system and assessed 
the effectiveness of relevant controls in the processes related to revenue reporting. 
We have reported identified deficiencies in the internal control system to management in 
writing. None of the identified deficiencies are considered to be significant.

procedures.
We performed control testing over the reconciliation between the accounting system and 
the terminal operating system as well as over unallocated cash and bank reconciliations.
We also performed testing over automated controls, such as calculations, segregation of 
duties, and others in the terminal operating system installed in the majority of in-scope 
terminals. For terminals operating on other systems, alternative substantive testing 
approach has been taken to ensure appropriate coverage.
For storage revenues, we obtained an understanding of customer contracts, relevant 
pricing and capacity mechanisms. On a sample basis, we tested customer agreements,

Impairment assessment of property, plant and equipment, joint ventures and associates
As per IAS 36, an entity shall assess at the end of each reporting period whether there is 
any indication that an asset may be impaired. Impairments are recognized when the 
carrying value is higher than the recoverable amounts. As per IAS 28, net investment in an 
associate or joint venture is impaired and impairment losses are incurred if, and only if, 
there is objective evidence of impairment as a result of one or more events that occurred 
after the initial recognition of the net investment (a 'loss event') and that loss event (or 
events) has an impact on the estimated future cash flows from the net investment that can 
be reliably estimated.
The Group controls a number of tank storage terminals with a total carrying value of 
owned property, plant and equipment of EUR 3,335.1 million as per 31 December 2025 
(note 3.3). Furthermore, the Group has an interest in a number of joint ventures and 
associates, with a total carrying value of EUR 2,112.8 million as per 31 December 2025 
(note 3.5). During the period, an impairment reversal of EUR 180.7 million was recognized 
for the Europoort CGU, and a full impairment of owned property, plant and equipment of 
EUR 30.2 million was recorded for Vopak Gas Terminal LLP ("VGT").
We focused on the impairment assessment of property, plant and equipment, joint 
ventures and associates, due to the size of the balances and because the impairment 
assessment on these balances performed by the Group included a variety of internal and 
external factors, which represents significant estimates. Those estimates required the use 
of valuation models, input data and assumptions by management, particularly with respect 
to determining future cash flows of the terminals (which are influenced by economic 
conditions, legislation and market dynamics), and the discount rates applied to the 
forecasted cash flows. Also, significant judgements are used by the Group in determining 
the CGU structure for the impairment assessment on property, plant and equipment.
For oil related assets, additional uncertainty arises from the energy transition and its 
impact on the forecasted cash flows. The Group treats its oil terminals as important but 
transitional assets. 
A change in these assumptions, based on their sensitivity, could have a significant effect 
on the financial statements. Given the complexity and the inherent subjectivity particularly 
related to the significant assumptions and the resulting significant estimation uncertainty, 
there is an inherent risk of overstatement of assets. Therefore, we considered this area as 
a key audit matter for our audit.
Our audit work and observations
We obtained an understanding of policies and internal controls for identifying impairment 
and impairment reversal triggers across terminal assets, joint ventures and associates.
We validated the Cash-Generating Units (“CGUs”) structure based by the Group, in line 
with IAS 36 and reviewed the impairment (reversal) trigger assessment Vopak performed 
across all CGUs. We have also reviewed the assessment performed by management in line 
with IAS 28 in order to identify whether there are any loss events that have an impact on 
the estimated future cash flows for the net investment in Joint Ventures and Associates 
and could result in an impairment loss.
For CGUs where an impairment (reversal) trigger was identified, we obtained 
management’s impairment assessment and evaluated the Value in Use (“ViU”) model, 
including significant assumptions, data inputs, terminal-specific factors, and the 
methodologies used. We challenged management’s assumptions in forecasts for:
We involved PwC valuation specialists to validate the discount rate applied by the Group in 
the impairment assessment and the terminal value assumption. We found the assumptions 
used to be in line with our expectations and they are applied consistently.
For the discount rate, inflation rate and terminal value used in the ViU calculations we 
performed a sensitivity analysis to calculate the degree to which these assumptions would 
need to move to impact the impairment (reversal) calculation. We also assessed 
management estimate of Fair Value Less Cost of Disposal ("FVLCD") for the relevant 
CGUs.
Furthermore, we assessed whether the main assumptions and related uncertainties are 
appropriately reflected in the disclosures in the financial statements.
Lastly, we assessed the energy transition scenario for the cash flow forecast in line with 
Vopak’s Sustainability Roadmap as approved by the Supervisory Board.

outside the formal materiality thresholds.

business model.
Unless otherwise specified (for example, in relation to tax disclosures), data and

operational control boundary as described under General disclosures and materiality.
Waste and circularity
Circularity
Responsible management of waste and wastewater is an important aspect of responsible 
business conduct. By minimizing our waste streams, we reduce the demand for natural 
resources and decrease our GHG emissions, specifically, upstream and downstream Scope 
3 emissions associated with resource extraction, processing, and end-of-life treatment.
At Vopak, circularity and waste treatment align with "cradle to grave” principles, reflecting 
our commitment to reducing waste and promoting its reuse during the construction, 
operation, and demolition phases of our assets:
Following a screening of our assets and activities, we have determined that the impacts, 
risks, and opportunities (IROs) related to resource use and circular economy, as outlined in 
ESRS 2 IRO-1 and described in paragraph 11, are not material to our organization. Our 
operations and value chain do not rely heavily on resource-intensive processes, nor do 
they generate significant waste streams. Therefore, further detailed disclosure regarding 
the processes for identifying material IROs  related to resource use and circular economy 
is not applicable. In conclusion, ESRS E5 – Resource Use and Circular Economy is 
considered to be not material for Vopak.
Waste management
In 2025, our water management activities included the treatment of 2.2 million cbm of 
water in wastewater treatment plants - on site (compared to 3 million cbm in 2024). This 
included water from cleaning processes, pumped contaminated groundwater, and 
collected rainwater, the majority of which was rainwater. Much of our rainwater is not 
collected separately and all our wastewater is therefore treated at wastewater treatment 
plants - on site. The quality of discharged water from our wastewater treatment plants 
meets the requirements set in our local permits.
In addition, Vopak actively invests in the construction, operation, and upgrading of 
wastewater treatment plants, such as the removal of PFAS from wastewater in our Belgium 
terminal.

Climate change adaptation
Introduction
Vopak has a climate transition plan that sets out how we will achieve our climate targets 
whilst developing and implementing technologies and infrastructure to support the broader 
energy transition. We acknowledge the assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on 
Climate Change (IPCC) that human influence is clear and physical impacts are already 
being felt. There is a growing need for governments, businesses, and citizens to adapt to 
and mitigate the impacts and risks of climate change.
In this section, we provide transparency on the resilience of our climate transition plan, 
considering both transition risks to our business model and strategy, and physical risks to 
our assets and operations. Please refer to Note 2. Climate change and energy in the 
sustainability statement for more details about wider aspects of our climate transition plan, 
including current GHG emissions and targets.
Our approach to managing climate-related risks and opportunities for Vopak
Identifying threats and opportunities from climate change is a key part of Vopak’s strategic 
planning cycle. Identification of climate-related risks is integrated within our enterprise risk 
management processes. Please refer to the Governance, risk & compliance section for 
more information.
Since 2017, we have developed our climate risk reporting in line with the Financial Stability 
Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosure (TCFD) framework. TCFD - as a 
standalone reporting framework - has been disbanded, and its work incorporated within 
the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB).  Main elements of the TCFD 
framework are also present within ESRS E1 reporting requirements. We have progressively 
evolved our reporting in line with these developments, and ensured that climate-related 
risks and opportunities are fully considered within our strategy, growth plans, and asset 
portfolio, including all new acquisitions and projects.
These evaluations consider:
Climate-related risks and opportunities
Transition risks and opportunities (ESRS E1-1, ESRS 2 SBM 3, ESRS 2 IRO 1)
Transition risks relate to the global shift towards a low-carbon economy and include 
changes in policies, regulations, product development, and market dynamics. These 
factors are thoroughly assessed regularly to ensure alignment with evolving environmental 
and economic landscapes.
To assess transition risks, we consider three scenarios prepared by the International 
Energy Agency (IEA, World Energy Outlook 2025) that predict future energy consumption 
and CO  emissions:
International Energy Agency (IEA) transition risk scenarios, such as shifts in energy 
policies and technology.
•
Physical risk assessments based on IPCC scenarios, including acute events such as 
floods and chronic changes such as rising sea levels.
•
Specific analysis by local or governmental bodies/research institutes.•
Vopak’s own business strategy planning.•
2
Current Policy Scenario (CPS): Anticipates a 2.9° Celsius rise in global temperatures – 
includes only the current policies that affect energy markets. Annual global energy- 
related CO  emissions rise slightly from current levels and approach 40 gigatons of CO
per year in the early 2030s, remaining around this level through to 2050. Emissions fall in 
aggregate in advanced economies, most substantially in Europe, and decline in China 
from 2030 onwards, but they increase elsewhere. Total GHG emissions lead to a global 
average surface temperature rise of around 2 °C in 2050 and 2.9 °C in 2100.
•
2 2 
Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS): Anticipates a 2.5° C rise in global temperatures – 
includes current policies and announced intentions. Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) is 
an exploratory scenario, designed to reflect the prevailing direction of travel for the 
energy system based on a detailed reading of country-specific energy, climate, and 
related industrial policies that have been adopted or put forward, even if not yet codified 
in law. It reflects the state of technology and market conditions but does not include 
aspirational goals. Energy-sector CO  emissions peak near term at just over 38 gigatons 
(Gt), falling to 35 Gt by the mid-2030s and below 30 Gt by 2050 – a level last seen in 
2005 – driven mainly by reduced coal use in China’s power sector. By 2100, the global 
temperature is projected to rise by 2.5 °C.
•
2
Net Zero Emissions Scenario (NZE): The IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario 
translates the 1.5 °C goal into a global pathway for the energy sector. The NZE Scenario 
is based on four central pillars that are widely applicable: clean energy electrification, 
energy efficiency, low-emissions fuels, and methane abatement. The updated NZE 
Scenario reflects the fact that exceeding 1.5 °C is now inevitable, and some reliance on 
technologies to remove CO  from the atmosphere is unavoidable to return warming to 
below 1.5 °C. In the NZE Scenario, the global average temperature increase falls back 
below 1.5 °C by 2100.
•

Impact of transition risks for Vopak
The global effort to combat climate change and lower CO  emissions is reshaping energy 
markets. While the pace and scale of this transformation remain uncertain, the impact on 
Vopak is direct; the products it manages are central to the energy and manufacturing 
sectors. As a result, these markets are in a state of constant flux, driven by the following:
The manufacturing market is another important segment for Vopak, with large volumes of 
feedstocks handled by our hub and industrial terminals. Current feedstocks include crude 
and naphtha. In the future, LC alternatives such as renewable naphtha, pyrolysis oil, and 
other sustainable alternatives will be added. Many manufacturing and industrial clusters 
are investing in decarbonization of products and processes. This presents Vopak with a 
wide range of business opportunities, including the handling of LC feedstocks, and LC 
hydrogen and CO  storage.
Most LC alternatives to traditional liquid hydrocarbon fuels exhibit a lower volumetric 
energy density. This means that, when substituting existing products, significantly greater 
storage volume and infrastructure are required to achieve an equivalent energy output, 
impacting demand for storage infrastructure. There are limits inherent to the amount of 
used cooking oil that can be generated, and the production of biofuels is limited by factors 
including land availability and competition with food chains. Synthetic and/or e-fuels can 
be very similar to these LC products but do not have the same limits. Vopak remains well 
positioned for the transition to these new energies although the timing of the transition will 
be different depending on the location and customers served.
As an early adopter of CSRD legislation, Vopak is also well placed to respond to future 
climate risk reporting requirements in other geographical jurisdictions, for example the 
proposed California Air Resources Board (CARB) legislation in California, USA.
Physical risks (ESRS E1/ESRS 2-IRO 1-20b)
Physical risks include acute risks, such as the increased frequency and intensity of 
extreme weather events, and chronic risks, such as rising sea levels, temperature shifts, 
fires, and changes in precipitation patterns. These risks are evaluated annually to ensure 
proactive management and adaptation. Our analysis focuses on our terminal operations 
and excludes our value chain (such as suppliers or customers). No significant physical or 
transition risks in relation to our terminals have been excluded from the analysis.
2
Global transition and decarbonization: Markets are fundamentally reshaped by global 
efforts to combat climate change and lower CO  emissions. The rise of carbon taxes and 
trading schemes in roughly 60% of the countries where Vopak operates is expected to 
increase our operational costs, as we continue to use fossil fuels. Industrial clusters will 
decarbonize through, for instance, CCUS, the use of low-carbon (LC) and recycled 
feedstocks, as well as LC energy, including hydrogen.
•
2
Shift to Lower-Carbon Products: This transition drives demand for new energy 
infrastructure (hydrogen, ammonia, battery solutions ) and lower-carbon alternatives 
including biofuels which often require handling more volume due to lower energy 
density. Despite the rise of renewables and the ongoing energy transition, global oil and 
gas demand is still forecasted to continue growing. Short- to medium-term oil product 
demand is forecasted to keep rising, fueled by steady consumption in mature markets 
and growth due to economic expansion in non-OECD nations.
•
Energy transition infrastructure: Vopak is strategically adapting its portfolio to focus on 
new energy transition and manufacturing end-markets to replace the changing nature of 
traditional energy demand. Power (electricity) demand is expanding with a growing share 
of intermittent renewable energy sources making battery storage solutions more 
important. For manufacturing sector customers, feedstock flexibility will be increasingly 
important with more recycling, renewables and other LC products being used.
•
Geopolitical volatility: Geopolitical tensions and sanctions underline the importance of 
security of supply and drive demand for storage of traditional storage demand for 
traditional products, influencing flow patterns and potentially delaying some expected 
refinery closures. Global economic growth is expected to be impacted by prolonged 
uncertainty, national security concerns, and protectionism. India, countries in Africa, and 
the Middle East are projected to grow faster, driven by growing populations.
•
Business case for gas infrastructure: The business case for regasification projects has 
gained new urgency due to expected sustained lower LNG prices. Lower LNG costs are 
lowering the "barrier to entry" for import value chains that were previously more difficult 
to unlock on account of affordability. However, this momentum faces a significant 
structural bottleneck: a tightening supply chain for gas turbines, where current lead 
times mean a 2026 investment will not yield operational capacity until 2031.
•
Simultaneously, the market is pivoting toward long-term supply diversification. Despite 
expected potential oversupply, the need for supplier diversification and long investment 
cycles is leading to a continued interest if global investments in further liquefaction 
•
capacity. Consequently, large-scale projects will remain strategic priorities for 
businesses seeking to balance global portfolios against shifting trade flows.
Low-carbon alternatives: LC alternatives are being added to the traditional product mix 
including (advanced) biofuels (e.g., ethanol, biodiesel, biomethanol), SAF, and ammonia, 
as well as synthetic and E-fuels. LC products are often blended with traditional fuels; for 
instance, a LC Synthetic Blend Component (SBC) is mixed with traditional jet fuel to 
make SAF. This means that the transition towards LC alternatives will be gradual.

To assess the physical climate-related risks, in 2025, we reassessed the 2024 outcome of 
the potential impact of three IPCC scenarios for 2050, which are based on global warming 
of 1.5° to 2° (RCP 2.6), 3.5° to 5° (RCP 4.5), and 5° Celsius (RCP 8.5). In 2025, global 
temperature rise to date was measured at 1.6° Celsius. According to the latest CO
emission report (NASA, June 2025), the concentration in the atmosphere was 430 ppm. 
Under the Paris Agreement, countries agreed to keep long-term global average surface 
temperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 
1.5°C by the end of this century. Current policies in place around the world are projected 
to result in approximately 2.6°C (IPCC) to 2.9°C (IEA) warming above pre-industrial levels 
by 2100.
In our sensitivity analyses, we have assessed the following acute and chronic climate 
impacts posing the highest risk to our current assets by 2050:
Heavy rainfall and river flooding: Terminals situated in low-lying coastal regions or near 
rivers face heightened flood risks due to rising sea levels, storm surges, and increased 
rainfall intensity.
Our assessment also considered the impact of sea level rise, which is expected to be up to 
0.5 meters by 2050 in places such as the US Gulf Coast. With regard to river flooding, we 
are monitoring how our assets can be better protected.
Increasing intensity of tropical storms and hurricanes: Regions prone to hurricanes and 
typhoons are experiencing more severe storms with stronger winds and heavier rainfall.
Excessive heat: Rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves can impact operational 
efficiency, equipment performance, and employee health and safety.
Increasing wind force and strong currents: Higher wind speeds, even under normal

Pay Metrics
Gender pay gap analysis (ESRS S1-5)
In line with our diversity and inclusion policies, we aim for a pay practice that is consistent 
and free from discrimination, regardless of personal factors. We monitor the salaries 
between men and women carefully. In 2024, we began reporting our gender pay gap data 
in preparation for the Pay Transparency Directive.
The analysis included employees in all entities under Vopak's operational control that are 
using our Global HR Platform. The gender pay gap percentage is calculated using the 
formula: (Average male annual salary - average female annual salary) / Average male 
annual salary.
The results for 2025 indicated a minimal 0.85% gender pay gap between male and female 
employees at Vopak.
In order to further improve pay consistency, Vopak started implementing a Global Job 
Level Framework project during 2025 to create consistency in job and salary levels across 
the organization. This project will be finalized during 2026.
CEO pay ratio (ESRS S1-6)
Each year, Vopak discloses this ratio to communicate how the CEO’s total remuneration 
compares to that of the average Vopak employee globally. 
In accordance with ESRS S1-6 and the 2021 Dutch Corporate Governance Code, the 
assessment includes all the remuneration components of the CEO’s total compensation 
package including:
To create a fair and representative reference point, we include our entire global base of 
own employees. We determine the average annual remuneration of our full-time workforce 
by taking the total wage costs of all subsidiaries, dividing them by the average number of 
hired Full-Time Equivalents (‘own employees’).

Responsible taxation
Vopak’s approach to taxation
Introduction
At Vopak, we believe that our responsibility extends beyond our operational and financial 
performance to encompass a meaningful contribution to the societies in which we operate. 
We view the taxes we pay not merely as a cost of doing business, but as an investment in 
the public infrastructure, education, and social services that enable communities to thrive 
and economies to grow. Our success is intrinsically linked to the stability and prosperity of 
the regions where our employees, customers, and partners live and work. Therefore, a 
responsible and transparent approach to taxation is highly relevant to our corporate 
purpose and our commitment to long-term, sustainable value creation.
Our approach to taxation is governed by our Global Tax Policy. In 2025, we reassessed 
and redefined the company’s approach to taxation and updated the Global Tax Policy and 
Principles in response to the changing (tax) environment. The approach to taxation was 
reviewed and approved by the EB of Vopak and subsequently presented to and discussed 
with the Audit Committee of the Supervisory Board. Our approach to taxation serves as a 
guiding framework for all consolidated entities within the Vopak Group and how Vopak 
operates with customers, suppliers, contractors, and employees.
The Senior Vice President Global Tax reviews Vopak’s approach to taxation annually, 
considering any changes in Vopak’s purpose, values, ambitions, structure, and the broader 
tax landscape.
Additionally, the EB reviews and approves Vopak’s approach to taxation every three years 
or sooner if revised earlier. This ensures that our approach to taxation reflects our vision, 
business objectives, and changes in the tax landscape.
Vopak’s Global Tax Policy and Principles
Our Global Tax Policy and Principles is available on our website. We strive to be a 
responsible taxpayer, and with the Global Tax Policy and Principles we lay down the 
fundamentals of behaving responsibly. This is aligned with the Tax Governance Code of 
the Confederation of Netherlands Industry and Employers’ (VNO-NCW). We also adhere to 
GRI: 207.
Tax and ESG
We consider tax to be a relevant component of our wider ESG considerations. Please find 
below an explanation of how tax addresses specific environmental, social, and governance 
issues within Vopak.
Regarding the environment, taxes can impact a company’s environmental performance if 
governments use tax legislation to change certain behavior. For Vopak, this includes, for 
example, carbon taxation. Please refer to Note 2. Climate change and energy for more 
information on this topic.
With regards to social aspects, we believe that our tax payments contribute positively to 
the countries and communities in which we operate, in line with our Global Tax Policy. We 
acknowledge that our business relies on public services, and our tax payments contribute 
to the economic and social well-being of those communities. Vopak has implemented and 
complies with Pillar II of the OECD’s Global Minimum Tax Framework. Pillar II ensures fair 
taxation by introducing a minimum tax of 15% for multinational companies in every 
jurisdiction in which they operate. This reduces the possibilities of shifting profit towards 
lower-tax jurisdictions.
Following our double materiality assessment, Vopak has determined that other topics 
relating to the tank storage business are more material under CSDR than responsible 
taxation as Vopak considers taxation to be something that follows the business. However, 
Vopak and relevant stakeholders increasingly view tax governance as an important 
indicator in the overall governance performance assessment of a company. To address 
this, we voluntarily report Vopak’s approach to taxation and our tax governance as an 
entity-specific disclosure.

Tax governance, control, and risk management
Governance
Within Vopak, the EB is ultimately responsible for tax affairs, managed through the portfolio 
of the CFO. Under the responsibility of the CFO, an experienced tax team is accountable 
for the execution of the tax strategy and managing our worldwide tax position. The Global 
Tax team reports quarterly to the CFO and Audit Committee of the Supervisory Board. 
Topics that were discussed with the Audit Committee in 2025 were the renewed Global 
Tax Policy, updates on the refinancing of intercompany loans, and global tax developments 
impacting Vopak, such as the introduction of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the United 
States. The Audit Committee also reviews the sustainability report, including the 
responsible-taxation paragraph of the annual report. Please also refer to the Independent 
Auditor's report in this Annual Report.
The Global Tax team advises management and the business on the tax implications of 
intended decisions, performs appropriate tax planning to support business goals, and 
ensures compliance with all local and international tax laws. Local finance managers are 
responsible for tax positions and filings in their country and are assessed by the Global Tax 
team and local external tax advisors.
Tax control and risk management
Vopak aims to be a responsible taxpayer. We therefore aim to exercise control over our tax 
position worldwide. This requires the early identification and prudent management of tax 
risks, something that is managed through our internal Tax Risk Management Policy. Our 
approach to tax risk management is guided by our low risk appetite. While we recognize 
that tax risks are inherent in a global business of our scale and complexity, we avoid and 
eliminate tax risks that could damage our reputation, our relationships with stakeholders, 
and/or have a significant financial impact.
We recognize several types of tax risks:
Our risk response depends on the following factors: (i), type of risk; (ii), the likelihood and 
impact; and (iii), our risk appetite. For example, risks arising from a change in legislation are 
mitigated by following knowledge sessions to keep our tax knowledge up to date and 
talking with external tax advisors. Reporting risks are mitigated by reviewing tax positions 
and reconciliations.
Tax risks are monitored through our Tax Control Framework and our Tax Risk & 
Compliance Questionnaire. The risks and their corresponding actions are documented in 
this Tax Control Framework. This is part of Vopak’s Control Framework, which sets the 
standard for internal controls governing financial reporting at Vopak. Vopak’s Control 
Framework has a dedicated section stipulating the internal controls that enforce 
compliance with the Global Tax Policy and Principles.
There are extensive controls and procedures in place to achieve this position of control. 
These include the following:
These controls and procedures are designed to align and monitor our approach to tax with 
Vopak’s business purpose and strategy.
All Vopak employees are trained in our Code of Conduct to ensure they are sufficiently 
equipped to identify and address (tax) dilemmas when encountered. Vopak employees are 
encouraged to report serious concerns through the normal reporting channels, but they 
can also voice concerns outside these channels through the Vopak Speak Up policy.
Tax planning
Tax follows business. We only employ tax structures that are driven by commercial 
considerations, are aligned with business activity, and which have genuine substance. We 
declare profits and pay taxes where the economic activities occur. The arm’s length 
principle is applied in all cross-border transactions and arrangements between Vopak 
Group entities, in line with OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises 
and Tax Administrations. This ensures Vopak contributes to the economic and social 
development in the countries in which we operate.
Reporting risks: the incorrect application of regulatory requirements;•
Compliance risks: too late, inaccurate or incomplete tax filings, reports or payments to 
tax authorities;
•
Changes in tax legislation risks;•
Sub-optimal tax positions.•
Standardization and documentation of tax processes;•
Review of existing and new business models, investments, acquisitions and divestments 
by tax specialists;
•
Weekly meetings between tax specialists in the global tax function to align tax topics, 
tax, and business developments;
•
Timely review and submission of tax returns and related documents and payments;•
Annual execution and monitoring of tax controls;•
Quarterly meetings with the CFO to discuss relevant tax topics and developments;•
Quarterly meetings with the Audit Committee of the Supervisory Board to discuss 
relevant strategic tax topics.

We do not control legal entities in countries that do not share tax information under tax 
information exchange agreements or legal entities in countries that are listed on the EU 
non-cooperative tax jurisdiction list. We do not control legal entities in low-tax-rate 
jurisdictions, no-tax jurisdictions or non-cooperative jurisdictions, unless there is 
substance, and the profits are generated by local economic activities. We do not control 
legal entities without commercial and/or economic activities solely for the purpose of tax 
avoidance (so-called tax havens).
We also focus on value creation by ensuring that our tax assets (e.g., tax losses, 
withholding tax credits) are utilized before expiry, and we optimize the use of available tax 
incentives (e.g., Investment Tax Credit in the United States) in accordance with both the 
letter and the spirit of tax laws and regulations.
Training
Given the fast-evolving tax landscape, our Global Tax team keeps on track of tax 
developments, new tax legislation and jurisprudence by following tax courses and 
workshops. During 2025, the Global Tax team followed various educational sessions on tax 
accounting, the United States' One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pillar II, and technological 
developments. They also spoke with external advisors on country specific topics such as 
the Debt Deduction Creation Rules in Australia and the new proposed indirect tax system 
in Brazil.
To increase tax awareness in the Vopak organization, the Global Tax team facilitated 
internal training sessions in 2025. These covered the quarterly completion of tax 
schedules, tax aspects of investment structures, transfer pricing, VAT, and payroll taxes. 
Upon request, the team provides topic-specific sessions.
Tax technology
We understand the importance of new developments in technology that can contribute to 
the continuing success of the company. It is vital for the tax function that it adopts tax 
technology and standardizes data and processes to improve the current way of working, 
make data-driven decisions, and to implement new legislation such as Pillar II and public 
country-by-country reporting.
To encourage progress on technological aspects within the tax department, the Global Tax 
team developed a tax technology roadmap in 2025. This roadmap sets out areas that 
qualify for technological improvement, such as data management and automated 
reporting, and subsequently prioritizes the improvements identified.
Relationship with tax authorities
We seek to build and maintain open, honest and constructive relationships with tax 
authorities in all jurisdictions in which we operate. We strive to engage with tax authorities, 
disclosing all relevant facts and seeking to resolve issues in a collaborative manner. Vopak 
tries to enter into cooperative compliance programs with tax authorities and, when 
possible, seeks upfront certainty on tax treatments through tax rulings or agreements.
In the Netherlands, we meet the Dutch tax authorities regularly to discuss relevant 
business developments. We also agree on a monitoring plan every year. We have a 
transparent relationship with the Dutch tax authorities and if any anomalies occur, we 
discuss these with them upfront, providing full disclosure.
Stakeholder engagement and advocacy
We value the ongoing constructive dialogue on tax matters with tax authorities, 
governments, majority shareholders, business groups, and/or civil society to ensure our 
approach to taxation continues to be aligned with evolving societal expectations and to 
support the development of effective tax systems, legislation, and administration. This 
ongoing dialogue is essential for Vopak to build and maintain a strong social license to 
operate.
For example, the Global Tax Department meets regularly with its majority shareholder, HAL 
Holding N.V., to discuss the tax topics relevant for the Vopak Group and the HAL group. 
During 2025, we had several meetings to discuss the Pillar II implications for Vopak and the 
total HAL Group, and the compliance aspects of Pillar II.
Vopak is a member of and participates in tax meetings at the Confederation of Netherlands 
Industry and Employers (VNO-NCW) to advocate and support tax transparency and fair 
taxation. We comply with the principles set out in the VNO-NCW Tax Governance Code 
and the Tax Transparency Benchmark of the Dutch Association of Investors for 
Sustainable Development (VBDO). We ensure that our approach to tax is aligned with 
these principles and expectations.
We support tax working groups at VNO-NCW that publicly advocate for tax transparency 
and fair taxation. We support the harmonization of overlapping international regulations if 
possible, such as the Pillar II regulation, for example.

External Benchmarks
Engaging in sustainability ratings and benchmarks offers a valuable opportunity to gauge 
our disclosures and performance relative to other companies, fostering a culture of 
continuous improvement in data quality and quantity for stakeholders. With numerous 
ratings and benchmarks available, it is impractical to participate in all of them actively.
Therefore, we prioritize those that hold significance for both our stakeholders and 
ourselves, based on transparency, credibility, accessibility of information, comparability 
with industry peers, and relevance to our sector. This deliberate approach ensures that our 
participation aligns closely with our commitment to transparency and sustainability, 
promoting meaningful progress within our organization and beyond.
